sk: तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म ततोऽन्नमभिजायते अन्नात्प्राणो मनः सत्यं लोकाः कर्मसु चामृतम् ||
ro: tapasā · cīyate · brahma · tataḥ · annam · abhijāyate · annāt · prāṇaḥ · manaḥ · satyaṁ · lokāḥ · karmasu · ca · amṛtam ||
hi: तपसा (by tapas / तप से) ब्रह्म (Brahman) चीयते (is built up / संचित होता है)। ततः (from that) अन्नम् (food / matter) अभिजायते (is born)। अन्न से प्राण (life-breath), मनः (mind), सत्यम् (truth), लोकाः (worlds), और कर्मसु अमृतम् (in actions, immortality) [उत्पन्न होते हैं]।
en: By tapas (austerity), Brahman is built up (cīyate); from that, food/matter (anna) is born. From food [come] prāṇa, manas (mind), truth (satya), the worlds (lokāḥ), and immortality in actions (karmasu amṛtam).

ws.h: तप से / by austerity
ws.e: by tapas — the creative heat/discipline; here repeated for the third time in the Muṇḍaka (2.2.10, 3.1.5, 3.2.1) — the central pillar of the Upanishad's teaching

ws.h: संचित होता है / is built up / is piled up
ws.e: is built up — from √ci (to heap/pile); the Agnicayana (fire-altar ritual) metaphor — Brahman-knowledge is accumulated layer by layer through sustained practice

ws.h: कर्मों में अमरत्व / immortality in actions
ws.e: immortality in actions — the imperishable dimension within karmic activity; actions informed by Brahman-knowledge participate in the eternal; the fruit of all karma becomes amṛta when rooted in Brahman

gr: Triple repetition from 2.2.10 and 3.1.5: this mantra appears for the THIRD time in the Muṇḍaka — first at 2.2.10, then at 3.1.5, and now at 3.2.1. Three repetitions create a structural backbone for the Upanishad's final two Khaṇḍas. Why three? (1) Architectural function: each appearance marks a transition — from meditation-path (end of Muṇḍaka 2) to liberation-teachings (opening of 3.1) to the culminating 'Satyameva Jayate' section (opening of 3.2). (2) Oral mnemonic: in the oral transmission tradition, triple repetition was the strongest form of emphasis — 'what is said three times is true.' (3) Progressive depth: each repetition invites deeper understanding — the first time is cosmological (Brahman creates), the second is personal (the aspirant builds), the third is final (the truth is sealed). The transition: this verse opens Khanda 2, which will build from the knower's portrait (3.1.4, 3.1.8-9) to the Upanishad's most famous declaration — 'satyameva jayate' (truth alone prevails).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.1 — Third appearance of this verse (identical to 2.2.10 and 3.1.5). The triple repetition is the most emphatic structural device in the Muṇḍaka — no other verse is repeated three times. This underscores its centrality: the tapas-creation sequence is the Upanishad's core cosmological-soteriological statement. The word 'cīyate' (is piled up) connects to the Agnicayana ritual tradition — the building of the fire-altar described in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa and the Taittirīya Saṁhitā. The spiritual practice of the aspirant IS a kind of inner agnicayana — building up the altar of Brahman-knowledge within the heart.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — तीसरी बार पुनरुक्ति (third repetition) = अत्यन्त बल (utmost emphasis)। 'तपसा चीयते ब्रह्म' = ज्ञान-तप (knowledge-tapas) से ब्रह्म-साक्षात्कार (Brahman-realisation) संचित (accumulated) होता है। यह मन्त्र पूरे उपनिषद् का मेरुदण्ड (backbone) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says third repetition = utmost emphasis. 'Tapasā cīyate brahma' = through knowledge-tapas, Brahman-realisation is accumulated. This mantra is the backbone of the entire Upanishad.
advaita.ins: Said once — a teaching. Said twice — a reminder. Said three times — a truth the Upanishad wants you to carry forever. Build up Brahman within yourself through tapas. Everything flows from that — life, mind, truth, worlds, and the deathless spark in every action.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — तृतीय पुनरुक्ति = भगवद्-ज्ञान (God-knowledge) और भक्ति-तप (devotion-tapas) का सर्वोच्च बल। यह मन्त्र अन्तिम खण्ड (final section) का द्वार खोलता है — जहाँ सत्य (truth) और भगवत्-प्राप्ति (God-attainment) का वर्णन होगा।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says third repetition = supreme emphasis on God-knowledge and devotion-tapas. This mantra opens the final section — where truth and God-attainment will be described.
vishisht.ins: Three times the Upanishad tells you: build up God-knowledge through devotion. Because it's opening the final door now — the door to truth itself, to the path that leads to God. Listen carefully to what follows.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — तीन बार = चेतना-शक्ति (consciousness-force / tapas) की त्रि-स्तरीय कार्यप्रणाली: (1) सृष्टि (creation — Muṇḍaka 2), (2) अभ्यास (practice — 3.1), (3) सत्य-प्राप्ति (truth-attainment — 3.2)। एक ही शक्ति — तीन अनुप्रयोग (applications)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says three repetitions = the triple operation of consciousness-force (tapas): (1) creation (Muṇḍaka 2), (2) practice (3.1), (3) truth-attainment (3.2). One force — three applications.
aurobindo.ins: The same consciousness-force works at every level. It creates the universe. It builds your practice. And now — it opens the door to truth. Three times the mantra appears because consciousness operates at three scales — cosmic, personal, and ultimate.

dp.q: 🔍 The triple repetition — architecture of the Muṇḍaka
dp.a: This mantra's three appearances (2.2.10, 3.1.5, 3.2.1) form the structural skeleton of the Muṇḍaka's second half: First appearance (2.2.10): at the end of the meditation teachings. Context: after the bow-and-arrow meditation (praṇava = bow, ātmā = arrow, brahma = target) and the OM-meditation. Meaning: Brahman's tapas is the creative force — it produces everything from food to immortality. Application: cosmological. Second appearance (3.1.5): at the heart of the two-birds section. Context: between the parable of the two birds (3.1.1-4) and the bridge-verses (3.1.5-7). Meaning: the aspirant's tapas builds up Brahman-knowledge within. Application: personal/soteriological. Third appearance (3.2.1): at the opening of the final Khanda — the 'Satyameva Jayate' section. Context: the verse now stands as a gateway to the Upanishad's climactic teachings on truth, the path, and final liberation. Application: culminating/eschatological. The pattern: cosmological → personal → ultimate. The same tapas that creates the world empowers the individual and reveals the final truth. In oral tradition: triple repetition was the strongest mnemonic device — what is said three times becomes indelibly imprinted on the student's memory.

dp.q: 🔍 'Karmasu amṛtam' — immortality within action
dp.a: The phrase 'karmasu amṛtam' (immortality in actions) encapsulates a key Muṇḍaka teaching — that the eternal can be found within the temporal: The paradox: karma (action) is, by definition, finite — it has a beginning, a middle, and an end. How can amṛta (immortality/deathlessness) exist 'in' actions? The resolution: when actions are informed by Brahman-knowledge (tapas → brahma), they cease to be ordinary karma. They become expressions of the eternal within the temporal. The knower acts from Self-delight (ātma-krīḍa, ātma-rati — 3.1.4), and such action is not binding but liberating. Three levels of understanding: (1) Ritualistic: the Vedic rituals, when performed correctly, yield imperishable results — the 'immortality' of heavenly worlds. (2) Ethical: actions rooted in truth (satya) have an imperishable dimension — they participate in the cosmic order (ṛta). (3) Spiritual: the Brahman-knower's actions are amṛta because they arise from and return to the imperishable Self — there is no karma created, no bondage generated, no saṁsāra perpetuated. The Gītā's elaboration (4.24): 'brahmārpaṇaṁ brahma haviḥ brahmāgnau brahmaṇā hutam' — 'the offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman.' When everything is Brahman, every action is immortal.

sk: यः सर्वज्ञः सर्ववित्यस्य ज्ञानमयं तपः तस्मादेतद्ब्रह्म नाम रूपमन्नं च जायते ||
ro: yaḥ · sarva-jñaḥ · sarva-vit · yasya · jñāna-mayaṁ · tapaḥ · tasmāt · etat · brahma · nāma · rūpam · annaṁ · ca · jāyate ||
hi: जो (यः) सर्वज्ञ (omniscient) है, सर्ववित् (all-knowing) है, जिसका (यस्य) तप (tapas) ज्ञानमय (made of knowledge / ज्ञान-स्वरूप) है — उससे (तस्मात्) यह ब्रह्म (Vedic creative principle), नाम (name), रूप (form), और अन्न (food/matter) जायते (is born)।
en: He who is omniscient (sarva-jña), all-knowing (sarva-vit), whose tapas (tapaḥ) is made of knowledge (jñāna-mayam) — from Him are born this Brahman, name (nāma), form (rūpa), and food (anna).

ws.h: सर्वज्ञ / omniscient
ws.e: omniscient — sarva (all) + jña (knowing); knows everything simultaneously; cf. Śvetāśvatara 3.19: 'apāṇi-pādo javano grahītā paśyaty acakṣuḥ' — He perceives without senses

ws.h: सब का ज्ञाता / all-knowing / knower of all
ws.e: all-knowing — sarva + √vid (to know); while sarva-jña = knowing all facts, sarva-vit = knowing the essence/nature of all things; the distinction is between knowledge of things and knowledge of the thing-in-itself

ws.h: ज्ञान-स्वरूप तप / tapas made of knowledge
ws.e: tapas whose very substance is knowledge — jñāna (knowledge) + maya (made of/consisting of) + tapas (creative heat/austerity); Brahman's creative force is not blind energy but intelligent will; cf. 1.1.9: 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ'

ws.h: नाम और रूप / name and form
ws.e: name and form — the twin principles of differentiation; nāma = the conceptual identity of things; rūpa = their sensory appearance; the entire phenomenal world = nāma-rūpa (name-and-form)

gr: A variant of 2.2.11 and 3.1.6: this mantra closely parallels (though is not identical to) the earlier repetitions. The key difference: where 2.2.11/3.1.6 had 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ' (endowed with all glory) and 'tat etat satyam' (this is the truth), this verse has 'yasya jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' (whose tapas is made of knowledge). The significance of the variation: by swapping 'sarva-lakṣmī-maya' for 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ,' the Muṇḍaka connects back to its very first use of this phrase (1.1.9) — creating a ring-composition: the phrase introduced at the beginning of the Upanishad returns near its end. 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — 'tapas made of knowledge': Brahman's creative force is not blind heat or mechanical energy. It is jñāna-maya — made of, consisting of, saturated with knowledge. Creation is an act of intelligence, not chance. The nāma-rūpa teaching: from Brahman arise 'nāma' (name = conceptual identity) and 'rūpa' (form = sensory appearance). The entire phenomenal world is nāma-rūpa — the play of names and forms upon the unchanging substrate of Brahman.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.2 — This verse is a variant of 2.2.11 and 3.1.6, with the significant substitution of 'yasya jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' for 'sarva-lakṣmī-mayaḥ … tat etat satyam.' The phrase 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' first appeared at 1.1.9 — its reappearance here creates a ring-composition (inclusio) spanning the entire Upanishad. The nāma-rūpa distinction is a fundamental Upanishadic concept: Chāndogya 6.3.2-3 describes how the three elements (fire, water, earth) differentiate into nāma-rūpa through their combinations. Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.7: 'This [universe] was then undifferentiated; it became differentiated by name and form.' The Muṇḍaka places nāma-rūpa as emanating from Brahman — the entire classified, named, formed world is Brahman's self-expression.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' = ब्रह्म का तप = शुद्ध ज्ञान (pure knowledge) — अन्ध ऊर्जा (blind energy) नहीं। 'नाम-रूप' = संसार = मिथ्या (illusory appearance) — ब्रह्म पर अध्यारोपित (superimposed on Brahman)। ब्रह्म = अधिष्ठान (substratum) — नाम-रूप = आभास (appearance)।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' = Brahman's tapas = pure knowledge — not blind energy. 'Nāma-rūpa' = the world = illusory appearance — superimposed on Brahman. Brahman = the substratum — nāma-rūpa = the appearance.
advaita.ins: Brahman's creative power isn't blind force — it's pure intelligence. From that intelligence arise all names and forms — everything you see, hear, touch. But names and forms are not Brahman itself — they're appearances on the unchanging screen of consciousness. Know the screen, and the movie can't deceive you.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' = भगवान् का तप = सर्वज्ञ संकल्प (omniscient will)। 'नाम-रूप' = सृष्टि = भगवान् का वास्तविक विकास (real transformation) — मिथ्या (illusion) नहीं। सृष्टि = भगवान् का शरीर (body of God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' = the Lord's tapas = omniscient will. 'Nāma-rūpa' = creation = the Lord's real transformation — not illusion. Creation = the body of God.
vishisht.ins: God creates with omniscient will — knowing everything that will emerge. Names and forms aren't illusions — they're God's real self-expression. The world is His body, and every named, formed thing is a real part of Him.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानमयं तपः' = सत्य-चेतना (truth-consciousness) — सच्चिदानन्द (sat-cit-ānanda) की सृजनात्मक शक्ति। 'नाम-रूप' = चेतना का विभेदन (differentiation of consciousness) — अवरोहण (involution) की प्रक्रिया — जिससे जड़ पदार्थ (matter / anna) तक पहुँचती है।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' = truth-consciousness — the creative power of sat-cit-ānanda. 'Nāma-rūpa' = the differentiation of consciousness — the process of involution — through which consciousness descends even to matter (anna).
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness creates through knowledge, not force. It differentiates itself into names and forms — not losing itself but expressing itself. From pure awareness to matter, every level is consciousness in a different mode. The tapas that creates is truth-consciousness, and everything it creates carries that truth within.

dp.q: 🔍 'Jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — the ring-composition of the Muṇḍaka
dp.a: The phrase 'jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' (tapas made of knowledge) creates a ring-composition spanning the entire Muṇḍaka Upanishad: First appearance (1.1.9): at the very beginning of the teaching, when the Upanishad introduces Brahman: 'yaḥ sarva-jñaḥ sarva-vit yasya jñāna-mayaṁ tapaḥ' — 'He who is omniscient, all-knowing, whose tapas is made of knowledge.' This is the thesis — the opening declaration. Final appearance (3.2.2): near the end of the Upanishad, the same phrase returns — closing the circle. The thesis is restated, now enriched by everything taught in between (the two kinds of knowledge, the fire-rituals, the bow-and-arrow meditation, the two birds, the knower's portrait, the river-ocean simile, 'brahma-vid brahmaiva bhavati'). What 'jñāna-maya tapas' means: (1) Brahman's creative force is intelligent, not mechanical — it is tapas whose very substance is jñāna (knowledge). (2) This distinguishes the Upanishadic view from both materialism (creation from blind matter) and voluntarism (creation from arbitrary will). Creation is the self-expression of omniscient consciousness. (3) The aspirant's tapas should mirror Brahman's tapas — it too should be 'jñāna-maya' — saturated with understanding, not mere mechanical austerity.

dp.q: 🔍 Nāma-rūpa — the philosophical significance of 'name and form'
dp.a: The pair 'nāma-rūpa' (name and form) is one of the most fundamental concepts in Upanishadic philosophy: What are nāma and rūpa? (1) Nāma (name) = the conceptual identity of a thing — what it is called, how it is classified, its place in the mental map of the world. Nāma is the principle of mental differentiation. (2) Rūpa (form) = the sensory appearance of a thing — its shape, colour, texture, the way it presents itself to the senses. Rūpa is the principle of perceptual differentiation. (3) Together, nāma-rūpa = the entire phenomenal world — every object, every being, every event has a name (conceptual identity) and a form (perceptual appearance). The Upanishadic teaching: nāma-rūpa is not self-existent — it arises FROM Brahman ('tasmāt … nāma rūpam … jāyate'). The world of differentiated things emerges from the undifferentiated Brahman, much as waves arise from the ocean. The waves are real AS waves, but they are ultimately water. Key parallels: (1) Chāndogya (6.3.2-3): the three elements (tejas, āpas, pṛthivī) differentiate into nāma-rūpa through their mutual combinations — the 'trivṛt-karaṇa' (triplication). (2) Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.4.7): 'This was then undifferentiated (avyākṛta); it became differentiated (vyākṛta) by nāma-rūpa.' (3) Buddhist parallel: nāma-rūpa appears as a link in the twelve-fold chain of dependent origination (pratītya-samutpāda) — though with a different metaphysical framework.

sk: तदेतत्सत्यं मन्त्रेषु कर्माणि कवयो यान्यपश्यंस्तानि त्रेतायां बहुधा सन्ततानि तान्याचरथ नियतं सत्यकामा एष वः पन्थाः सुकृतस्य लोके ||
ro: tat · etat · satyaṁ · mantreṣu · karmāṇi · kavayaḥ · yāni · apaśyan · tāni · tretāyāṁ · bahudhā · santatāni · tāni · ācaratha · niyataṁ · satya-kāmāḥ · eṣaḥ · vaḥ · panthāḥ · sukṛtasya · loke ||
hi: वह (तत्) यह (एतत्) सत्य (truth) है। मन्त्रों में (mantreṣu) कवियों (kavayaḥ / seers) ने जो कर्माणि (rites/actions) अपश्यन् (saw / perceived) — वे (तानि) त्रेतायां (in the Tretā fire / three-fold fire) बहुधा (in many ways) सन्ततानि (spread out / elaborated) हैं। उन्हें (तानि) नियतम् (steadily / faithfully) आचरथ (practise / perform), हे सत्यकामाः (lovers of truth / seekers of truth)! यह (एषः) तुम्हारा (वः) पन्थाः (path) है — सुकृतस्य लोके (to the world of good deeds / the world won by merit)।
en: This is the truth (tat etat satyam). The rites (karmāṇi) which the seers (kavayaḥ) saw (apaśyan) in the mantras — those are spread out (santatāni) in many ways (bahudhā) in the Tretā fire (tretāyām). Practise them (tāni ācaratha) faithfully (niyatam), O lovers of truth (satya-kāmāḥ)! This (eṣaḥ) is your (vaḥ) path (panthāḥ) to the world of merit (sukṛtasya loke).

ws.h: कवि / ऋषि / seers
ws.e: seers / poet-sages — kavi = one who 'sees' truth directly; the Vedic seers 'saw' the mantras — they did not compose them but perceived them in meditation

ws.h: त्रेता अग्नि में / in the threefold fire
ws.e: in the Tretā fire — the three Vedic fires: gārhapatya (household fire), āhavanīya (offering fire), dakṣiṇāgni (southern fire); the Vedic ritual system is 'spread out' across these three fires

ws.h: सत्य के इच्छुक / lovers of truth
ws.e: lovers of truth — satya (truth) + kāma (desire/love); those whose deepest desire is truth; cf. Chāndogya 4.4: Satyakāma Jābāla — the student whose love of truth was itself his qualification

ws.h: सुकृत (merit) के लोक (world) में
ws.e: in the world of good deeds / the world won by merit — the heavenly worlds attained through ritual action; this is the 'lower' path, valid but not the highest (cf. 1.2.7-10)

gr: Repetition from 2.2.8 and 3.1.7 — the ritual-path bridge: this mantra appears for the THIRD time — first at 2.2.8, then at 3.1.7, and now at 3.2.3. Like 3.2.1 (= 2.2.10, 3.1.5), it is part of the triple-bridge structure linking the Muṇḍaka's final sections. The ritual path: the Muṇḍaka is famous for distinguishing 'higher knowledge' (parā vidyā) from 'lower knowledge' (aparā vidyā) — 1.1.4-5. Yet it does not reject the ritual path outright. This repeated verse validates the karma-kāṇḍa path — 'practise them faithfully, O lovers of truth!' — while implicitly placing it below the jñāna path. The address to 'satya-kāmāḥ' (lovers of truth): the seeker is addressed with respect — they are not deluded or ignorant but 'lovers of truth.' The Upanishad honours their aspiration even while guiding them toward a higher path. 'Sukṛtasya loke' — 'the world of merit': the ritual path leads to merit-worlds (heaven/svarga). These are real attainments but temporary — the next mantras will point beyond them to the imperishable.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.3 — Third appearance (= 2.2.8, 3.1.7). This verse, like 3.2.1, appears three times — creating a pair of triple-repeated verses that form the structural scaffolding of the Muṇḍaka's final two Khaṇḍas. The ritual path described here is the 'aparā vidyā' (lower knowledge) path of 1.1.4-5 — valid, respected, but not the ultimate. The phrase 'satya-kāmāḥ' echoes the Chāndogya's Satyakāma (4.4.1-5) — the student whose very name means 'lover of truth' and whose truthfulness qualifies him for Brahman-knowledge. The 'tretā' (threefold fire) refers to the three Vedic sacrificial fires — gārhapatya, āhavanīya, dakṣiṇāgni — around which the entire śrauta ritual system is organised.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — कर्मकाण्ड-मार्ग (ritual path) = वैध (valid) किन्तु अपरा (lower)। 'सुकृतस्य लोके' = पुण्य-लोक — स्वर्ग — किन्तु अनित्य (temporary)। मन्त्र कर्मकाण्ड का सम्मान करता है — किन्तु अगले मन्त्र उससे ऊपर (beyond it) ले जाएँगे।
advaita.en: Shankara says the ritual path = valid but lower. 'Sukṛtasya loke' = worlds of merit — heaven — but temporary. The mantra respects the ritual path but the next mantras will lead beyond it.
advaita.ins: The ritual path is real and honoured — 'practise it faithfully, O lovers of truth!' But where does it lead? To the world of merit — which is temporary. What follows will show a path beyond — beyond merit, beyond worlds, to the imperishable itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — कर्मकाण्ड = भक्ति-मार्ग (devotional path) का अंग (limb)। 'सत्यकामाः' = भगवद्-प्रेमी (God-lovers)। कर्म-मार्ग = भगवद्-सेवा (service to God) — भगवान् को अर्पित (offered to God) हो तो श्रेष्ठ।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says ritual path = a limb of the devotional path. 'Satya-kāmāḥ' = God-lovers. Ritual path = service to God — if offered to God, it is excellent.
vishisht.ins: The rituals the seers saw — they're real paths. But offer them to God, and they become something more. Don't perform them for merit alone — perform them as service. That transforms the path from leading to heaven to leading to God.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'कर्माणि' = बाह्य अनुष्ठान (external rituals) — चेतना-विकास (consciousness-evolution) की प्रारम्भिक अवस्था। 'सत्यकामाः' = सत्य के अन्वेषक — जो सत्य चाहते हैं, उनके लिए कर्मकाण्ड प्रथम सोपान (first step)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'karmāṇi' = external rituals — an initial stage of consciousness-evolution. 'Satya-kāmāḥ' = seekers of truth — for those who want truth, ritual is the first step.
aurobindo.ins: The rituals are real — the seers saw them. But they're the first step, not the last. For you who love truth, begin here — with disciplined practice, with the threefold fire. But know that the path doesn't end at the world of merit. It continues upward.

dp.q: 🔍 The Muṇḍaka's treatment of ritual — respect without ultimacy
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka Upanishad has a distinctive relationship with Vedic ritual: The critique (1.2.7-10): in its first Muṇḍaka, the Upanishad delivers one of the sharpest critiques of ritual in Upanishadic literature — 'plavā hy ete adṛḍhā yajña-rūpāḥ' (1.2.7) — 'Frail indeed are those boats, the ritual forms.' Rituals are called 'frail boats' that cannot cross the ocean of saṁsāra. Those who delight in ritual are 'fools who think they have reached the highest' (1.2.9). The validation (3.2.3): yet THIS verse validates the ritual path — 'practise them faithfully, O lovers of truth!' How do we reconcile the critique with the validation? The resolution: (1) The critique targets those who mistake the ritual path for the highest — those who think ritual alone is sufficient. (2) The validation affirms the ritual path as a real path — it leads to 'sukṛtasya loke' (the world of merit). (3) But the Upanishad immediately follows this verse with teachings that point BEYOND the ritual path — to the imperishable, to Brahman, to 'satyameva jayate.' The pedagogical strategy: honour the student's current practice (ritual), affirm its validity, then gently lead them beyond it. This is the Upanishadic method — not rejection but transcendence.

dp.q: 🔍 'Satya-kāmāḥ' — the qualification of the seeker
dp.a: The address 'satya-kāmāḥ' (O lovers of truth) reveals the essential qualification for the spiritual path: What is satya-kāma? satya (truth) + kāma (desire/love) = one whose deepest desire is truth. Not one who merely studies truth, or talks about truth, or ritually invokes truth — but one who desires truth, who loves truth, whose fundamental orientation is toward the real. The Chāndogya's Satyakāma (4.4): the story of Satyakāma Jābāla is the locus classicus. When asked his lineage by the teacher Hāridrumata Gautama, Satyakāma honestly confesses that he doesn't know his father's name — his mother Jabālā told him she doesn't know. Gautama's response: 'None but a Brāhmaṇa could speak thus. Bring the fuel, my boy; I will initiate you. You have not swerved from truth.' Satyakāma's truthfulness IS his qualification — not birth, not learning, not ritual purity, but the love of truth. The Muṇḍaka's application: the students addressed as 'satya-kāmāḥ' are qualified by their desire — their love of truth. The path is open to those who genuinely seek. The Upanishad's confidence is: if you truly desire truth, the path will take you there — from ritual to knowledge, from merit-worlds to the imperishable.

sk: कामान्यः कामयते मन्यमानः स कामभिर्जायते तत्र तत्र पर्याप्तकामस्य कृतात्मनस्तु इहैव सर्वे प्रविलीयन्ति कामाः ||
ro: kāmān · yaḥ · kāmayate · manyamānaḥ · saḥ · kāmabhiḥ · jāyate · tatra · tatra · paryāpta-kāmasya · kṛta-ātmanaḥ · tu · iha · eva · sarve · pravilīyanti · kāmāḥ ||
hi: कामान् (desires / कामनाओं को) जो (यः) कामयते (desires / चाहता है) मन्यमानः (thinking [himself to be the doer/enjoyer] / अपने को कर्ता-भोक्ता मानता हुआ) — वह (सः) कामभिः (by/with desires / कामनाओं सहित) तत्र तत्र (here and there / यहाँ-वहाँ / विभिन्न योनियों में) जायते (is born / जन्म लेता है)। पर्याप्तकामस्य (of one whose desires are fulfilled / जिसकी कामनाएँ पूर्ण हो गई हैं) कृतात्मनः (of the self-realised one / कृतार्थ आत्मा वाले) तु (but / किन्तु) इह एव (right here / यहीं) सर्वे कामाः (all desires / सभी कामनाएँ) प्रविलीयन्ति (dissolve completely / पूर्णतया विलीन हो जाती हैं)।
en: He who desires desires (kāmān kāmayate), thinking [himself to be the agent] (manyamānaḥ) — he is born (jāyate) here and there (tatra tatra) along with [his] desires (kāmabhiḥ). But (tu) for the one whose desires are fulfilled (paryāpta-kāmasya), the self-realised one (kṛta-ātmanaḥ), all desires (sarve kāmāḥ) dissolve completely (pravilīyanti) right here (iha eva).

ws.h: अपने को [कर्ता/भोक्ता] मानता हुआ / thinking [himself to be the agent]
ws.e: thinking / considering oneself — present participle of √man (to think); the desirer 'thinks' he is the agent and enjoyer — this identification with the ego is the root cause of rebirth; cf. Gītā 3.27: 'ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā kartāham iti manyate'

ws.h: कामनाओं सहित / with/by desires
ws.e: with desires / driven by desires — instrumental plural; the jīva is born 'with' its desires — desires are the vehicle of rebirth; unfulfilled desires at death propel the soul into a new body suited to fulfil them

ws.h: जिसकी कामनाएँ पूर्ण हो गईं / one whose desires are fulfilled
ws.e: one whose desires are fully satisfied — paryāpta (sufficient/complete/fulfilled) + kāma (desire); not one who has suppressed desires but one who has found the Self — and in the Self, all desire is inherently fulfilled; synonymous with āpta-kāma (3.2.6)

ws.h: कृतार्थ आत्मा / self-realised / one who has accomplished the Self
ws.e: one whose Self is accomplished/realised — kṛta (done/accomplished) + ātman (Self); the Self-knower — one who has 'done the work' of Self-realisation; the task is complete, the goal is reached

ws.h: पूर्णतया विलीन हो जाती हैं / dissolve completely
ws.e: dissolve completely / merge away — pra + vi + √lī (to dissolve/merge); a strong verb — desires don't merely diminish or become dormant; they DISSOLVE entirely, like salt in water, leaving no residue

gr: Desire as the engine of rebirth — and its dissolution: this mantra presents one of the most psychologically precise teachings in the Muṇḍaka — desire (kāma) is the mechanism of rebirth, and its dissolution is liberation. The first half — the mechanism of rebirth: 'kāmān yaḥ kāmayate manyamānaḥ, saḥ kāmabhiḥ jāyate tatra tatra.' Three elements: (1) kāmān kāmayate — 'desires desires': the redundancy is deliberate — the desirer is caught in a loop of desiring desire itself. (2) manyamānaḥ — 'thinking [himself to be the agent]': the identification with the ego is the root — 'I' am the one who desires, 'I' am the one who enjoys. This 'manyamāna' (false identification) is what Shankara calls ahaṅkāra (ego-sense). (3) tatra tatra jāyate — 'is born here and there': the jīva is born in various wombs, various worlds, various conditions — driven by unfulfilled desires. Each life is shaped by the desires left over from the previous one. The second half — dissolution of desire: 'paryāpta-kāmasya kṛtātmanaḥ tu, ihaiva sarve pravilīyanti kāmāḥ.' The contrast is absolute: (1) paryāpta-kāma — desires are 'fulfilled/completed'. Not by satisfying every wish but by finding the Self — in which all desire is inherently satisfied. (2) kṛta-ātman — the Self is 'accomplished'. The inner work is done. (3) iha eva pravilīyanti — 'right HERE they dissolve.' Not in some future life, not in heaven, not after death — but RIGHT HERE, in this very body, in this very life. The dissolution is complete (pravilīyanti) and immediate (iha eva).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.4 — This verse closely parallels the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.6): 'tad eṣa śloko bhavati — tad yathā'hiṁ nirlvayanīṁ valmīke mṛtāṁ pratyastāṁ śayānām … kāmān yaḥ kāmayate manyamānaḥ, saḥ kāmabhir jāyate tatra tatra, paryāptakāmasya kṛtātmanas tu ihaiva sarve pravilīyanti kāmāḥ.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka context is Yājñavalkya's teaching on the post-mortem journey of the soul. The image of desire as the 'engine' of rebirth is also found in the Gītā (8.6): 'yaṁ yaṁ vāpi smaran bhāvaṁ tyajaty ante kalevaram, taṁ tam evaiti kaunteya sadā tad-bhāva-bhāvitaḥ' — 'Whatever state one remembers when leaving the body at the end, to that very state one goes.' The word 'pravilīyanti' (completely dissolve) is stronger than 'vilīyanti' — the prefix 'pra' intensifies the dissolution. The Chāndogya (8.12.6) similarly states: 'evam evaiṣa samprasādo'smāc charīrāt samutthāya paraṁ jyotir upasampadya svena rūpeṇābhiniṣpadyate' — 'Rising from this body, he attains the supreme light and emerges in his own form.'

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'मन्यमानः' = अहंकार (ego) — 'मैं कर्ता हूँ, मैं भोक्ता हूँ' — यह भ्रम (delusion) पुनर्जन्म (rebirth) का कारण। 'पर्याप्तकामस्य कृतात्मनः' = जिसने आत्मा को जाना — उसकी सभी कामनाएँ इहैव (right here) विलीन — पुनर्जन्म नहीं। कामना = बन्धन (bondage)। कामना-निवृत्ति = मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'manyamānaḥ' = the ego — 'I am the doer, I am the enjoyer' — this delusion is the cause of rebirth. 'Paryāpta-kāmasya kṛtātmanaḥ' = one who has known the Self — all desires dissolve right here — no rebirth. Desire = bondage. Cessation of desire = mokṣa.
advaita.ins: You desire — and you're reborn. Not because desire is punished, but because desire is the engine. Each unfulfilled wish pulls you into another body, another life, another round. But when you find the Self — the source of all satisfaction — every desire dissolves. Not in some future life. Right here. Right now. The engine stops.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'कामभिः जायते' = भगवान् से विमुख (turned away from God) जीव — कामनाओं द्वारा संसार-चक्र (cycle of rebirth) में घूमता है। 'पर्याप्तकामस्य' = भक्त जिसने भगवान् को प्राप्त किया — उसकी सब कामनाएँ तृप्त — भगवान् में सर्व-तृप्ति (all satisfaction in God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'kāmabhiḥ jāyate' = the soul turned away from God — cycles through rebirth driven by desires. 'Paryāpta-kāmasya' = the devotee who has attained God — all desires are satisfied — all satisfaction is in God.
vishisht.ins: Desire without God drives you from birth to birth. But when you find God, every desire finds its rest. Not because desires are crushed — because they're fulfilled. God is what every desire was secretly looking for. Find Him, and the search ends — right here, in this life.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'मन्यमानः' = अहंकार-चेतना (ego-consciousness) — सीमित 'मैं' (limited 'I')। 'कामभिः जायते' = इच्छा-शक्ति (desire-force) = चेतना का विकृत रूप (distorted form of consciousness) — जो पुनर्जन्म चक्र चलाता है। 'प्रविलीयन्ति' = चेतना-रूपान्तर (consciousness-transformation) से कामना विलीन — अहंकार गिरता है, चेतना मुक्त।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'manyamānaḥ' = ego-consciousness — the limited 'I'. 'Kāmabhiḥ jāyate' = desire-force = a distorted form of consciousness — which drives the cycle of rebirth. 'Pravilīyanti' = through consciousness-transformation, desire dissolves — the ego falls, consciousness is free.
aurobindo.ins: Desire is consciousness in distorted form — the ego grasping at objects, thinking itself the doer. This distortion drives rebirth. But when consciousness transforms — when you see through the ego to the Self behind it — desire doesn't need to be killed. It dissolves. Because what desire was reaching for, you already are.

dp.q: 🔍 'Kāmān kāmayate' — the loop of desire and rebirth
dp.a: The phrase 'kāmān yaḥ kāmayate' ('he who desires desires') reveals the mechanism of rebirth with remarkable precision: The loop: (1) Desire arises → (2) The ego identifies with the desire ('manyamānaḥ') → (3) Action follows desire → (4) Karmic seeds are sown → (5) Death comes with unfulfilled desires → (6) The unfulfilled desires propel the soul into a new body ('tatra tatra jāyate') → (7) In the new body, desire arises again → repeat. Why 'manyamānaḥ' is the key: the mantra doesn't say desire alone causes rebirth — it says desire PLUS 'manyamānaḥ' (thinking oneself to be the agent/enjoyer). This is crucial: it's not desire per se that binds — it's desire combined with ego-identification. The Gītā (3.27) makes the same point: 'prakṛteḥ kriyamāṇāni guṇaiḥ karmāṇi sarvaśaḥ, ahaṅkāra-vimūḍhātmā kartāham iti manyate' — 'Actions are performed by the guṇas of prakṛti, but the one deluded by ego thinks: I am the doer.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka parallel (4.4.5-6): Yājñavalkya's teaching is virtually identical — 'As is one's desire (kāma), so is one's will (kratu); as is one's will, so is one's deed (karma); as is one's deed, so is one's destiny (gati).' Desire → will → action → destiny → rebirth. 'Tatra tatra' — 'here and there': the desirer is born in many places — human, animal, divine, hellish — according to the nature of the desires. The variety of births reflects the variety of desires.

dp.q: 🔍 'Ihaiva sarve pravilīyanti kāmāḥ' — liberation is here, not elsewhere
dp.a: The phrase 'iha eva sarve pravilīyanti kāmāḥ' ('right HERE all desires dissolve completely') makes a radical claim — liberation happens in this very life, not after death: 'Iha eva' — right here: the emphasis is unmistakable — 'iha' (here) + 'eva' (indeed/only). Not in heaven, not in a future life, not after death — but HERE, in this body, in this life. This is the Upanishadic concept of jīvan-mukti (liberation while living) — one need not wait for bodily death to be free. 'Pravilīyanti' — dissolve completely: the verb is emphatic. 'Pra-vi-lī' = to dissolve utterly, to merge away without residue. Desires don't merely weaken, become dormant, or go underground. They DISSOLVE — like salt in water, like mist in sunlight. Nothing remains. How do desires dissolve? Not by suppression — suppressed desires remain latent and resurface. Not by exhaustion — satisfying desires only creates more desires. But by fulfilment at the source. The Self IS the source of all satisfaction. Every desire is ultimately a desire for the Self — for completeness, for wholeness, for peace. When the Self is found (kṛta-ātman), the root from which all desires grow is reached. And when the root is reached, the branches (individual desires) naturally fall away. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka's beautiful image (4.4.7): 'As the slough of a snake lies on an ant-hill, dead and cast off, so lies this body. But that which is bodiless, immortal, prāṇa — that is Brahman, that is light.' When desires dissolve, what remains is not emptiness but fullness — the light of the Self.

sk: सत्येन लभ्यस्तपसा ह्येष आत्मा सम्यग्ज्ञानेन ब्रह्मचर्येण नित्यम् अन्तःशरीरे ज्योतिर्मयो हि शुभ्रो यं पश्यन्ति यतयः क्षीणदोषाः ||
ro: satyena · labhyaḥ · tapasā · hi · eṣaḥ · ātmā · samyag-jñānena · brahmacaryeṇa · nityam · antaḥ-śarīre · jyotir-mayaḥ · hi · śubhraḥ · yaṁ · paśyanti · yatayaḥ · kṣīṇa-doṣāḥ ||
hi: सत्येन (by truth / सत्य से), तपसा (by tapas / तप से), सम्यग्ज्ञानेन (by right knowledge / सम्यक् ज्ञान से), ब्रह्मचर्येण नित्यम् (by constant brahmacarya / निरन्तर ब्रह्मचर्य से) — यह (एषः) आत्मा (Self) लभ्यः (is attainable / प्राप्त होने योग्य) है। अन्तःशरीरे (within the body / शरीर के भीतर) ज्योतिर्मयः (made of light / ज्योतिर्मय) शुभ्रः (pure / resplendent) — जिसे (यं) यतयः (ascetics / साधक / strivers), क्षीणदोषाः (whose faults are destroyed / दोष-मुक्त), पश्यन्ति (see / दर्शन करते हैं)।
en: By truth (satyena), by tapas (tapasā), by right knowledge (samyag-jñānena), by constant brahmacarya (brahmacaryeṇa nityam) — this Self (eṣa ātmā) is attainable (labhyaḥ). Within the body (antaḥ-śarīre), [It is] made of light (jyotir-maya), pure/resplendent (śubhra) — which the ascetics (yatayaḥ), whose faults are destroyed (kṣīṇa-doṣāḥ), see (paśyanti).

ws.h: सत्य से / by truth
ws.e: by truth — the first of four qualifications; truth (satya) is the foundational prerequisite — without truthfulness, no spiritual attainment is possible; echoes 'satya-kāmāḥ' (lovers of truth) from 3.2.3

ws.h: सम्यक् ज्ञान से / by right knowledge
ws.e: by right knowledge — samyak (correct/complete/proper) + jñāna (knowledge); not any knowledge but 'right' knowledge — correct understanding of the Self, not mere book-learning or intellectual grasp

ws.h: ब्रह्मचर्य से / by brahmacarya
ws.e: by brahmacarya — literally 'conduct in Brahman' (brahma + carya); includes celibacy/sexual restraint but is broader — self-discipline, conservation of vital energy, living in accordance with the teacher's instruction

ws.h: ज्योतिर्मय / made of light
ws.e: made of light — jyotis (light) + maya (made of); the Self is not illuminated by an external light — it IS light; cf. Kaṭha 2.2.15: 'na tatra sūryo bhāti' — neither sun, moon, stars, nor fire illumines that Self; by Its light everything else shines

ws.h: जिनके दोष नष्ट हो गए / whose faults are destroyed
ws.e: whose faults are destroyed — kṣīṇa (destroyed/exhausted) + doṣa (fault/defect); the seers of the Self are those whose inner impurities (kāma, krodha, lobha, moha, mada, mātsarya) have been worn away through practice

gr: The fourfold path to the Self: this mantra prescribes four means (sādhana) for attaining the Self: (1) satya (truth) — the moral foundation. Without truthfulness, knowledge cannot ripen. (2) tapas (austerity/discipline) — the transformative fire. The 'cīyate brahma' of the repeated verses now becomes personal practice. (3) samyag-jñāna (right knowledge) — correct understanding of the Self, distinct from mere intellectual comprehension. 'Samyak' (right/complete) qualifies the knowledge — partial, distorted, or merely theoretical knowledge won't suffice. (4) brahmacarya (celibacy/self-discipline) — the conservation and channelling of vital energy toward the goal. 'Antaḥ-śarīre jyotir-mayaḥ' — 'within the body, made of light': the Self is not in a distant heaven or a remote transcendence — it is RIGHT HERE, within the body, luminous and pure. The problem is not the Self's absence but our inability to see it — obscured by doṣa (faults). 'Kṣīṇa-doṣāḥ' — 'whose faults are destroyed': the qualification for seeing the Self is not intellectual brilliance but inner purity. The faults (desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy) are like dust on a mirror — remove them, and the mirror naturally reflects. This mantra is the foundation for the next — 'satyameva jayate.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.5 — This mantra prescribes the fourfold sādhana: satya, tapas, samyag-jñāna, brahmacarya. The four terms correspond roughly to the four traditional qualifications (sādhana-catuṣṭaya) of the Vedāntic aspirant, though the traditional list (viveka, vairāgya, ṣaṭ-sampatti, mumukṣutva) is a later systematisation. The phrase 'antaḥ-śarīre jyotir-mayaḥ' (within the body, made of light) connects to the Chāndogya's 'tadyatha citra-dīpaḥ' (3.13.7-8) — the 'light within' teaching. The Kaṭha (2.2.15) and Śvetāśvatara (6.14) both describe the Self as self-luminous — by whose light everything else shines. The phrase 'kṣīṇa-doṣāḥ' (whose faults are destroyed) is also found in the Śvetāśvatara (6.21) and anticipates the Buddhist 'kṣīṇāsrava' (one whose impurities are exhausted).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — चार साधन: (1) सत्य = नैतिक आधार। (2) तप = अन्तर्मुखता (inwardness) — इन्द्रिय-निग्रह (sense-restraint)। (3) सम्यग्ज्ञान = 'अहं ब्रह्मास्मि' (I am Brahman) का यथार्थ बोध। (4) ब्रह्मचर्य = वीर्य-रक्षा और शमदमादि। 'ज्योतिर्मयः' = आत्मा = स्वयंप्रकाश (self-luminous) — बाह्य प्रकाश की आवश्यकता नहीं।
advaita.en: Shankara says four means: (1) satya = moral foundation. (2) tapas = inwardness — sense-restraint. (3) samyag-jñāna = correct understanding of 'ahaṁ brahmāsmi' (I am Brahman). (4) brahmacarya = conservation of vital energy and mental disciplines. 'Jyotir-maya' = the Self = self-luminous — needs no external light.
advaita.ins: Four things will take you to the Self: truth, tapas, right knowledge, and brahmacarya. Not one alone — all four together. And what will you find? A light within your own body — not brought from outside but always there, always shining. You couldn't see it because your faults blocked the view. Remove them, and the light reveals itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सत्येन लभ्यः' = भगवान् सत्य से प्राप्त होते हैं — सत्य = भक्ति का मूल (root of devotion)। 'ज्योतिर्मयः' = भगवान् = दिव्य ज्योति — शरीर के भीतर अन्तर्यामी (inner controller) रूप में विराजमान। 'क्षीणदोषाः' = जिन भक्तों के दोष (कर्म-वासना, अज्ञान) नष्ट — वे भगवद्-दर्शन (vision of God) करते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'satyena labhyaḥ' = God is attained by truth — truth = the root of devotion. 'Jyotir-maya' = the Lord = divine light — dwelling within the body as the inner controller (antaryāmī). 'Kṣīṇa-doṣāḥ' = those devotees whose faults (karmic impressions, ignorance) are destroyed — they behold God.
vishisht.ins: God is attained by truth, by tapas, by right knowledge, by devoted discipline. He lives within your body as pure light — the inner controller. Those whose faults have been burned away by practice — they see Him. The light was always there. Your faults were the only veil.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — चार साधन = चेतना-शुद्धि (consciousness-purification) के चार आयाम: सत्य (truth-consciousness), तप (concentration of consciousness-force), सम्यग्ज्ञान (integral knowledge), ब्रह्मचर्य (consecration of being)। 'ज्योतिर्मयः' = अतिमानसिक प्रकाश (supramental light) — शरीर में अवतरित (descended into the body)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says four means = four dimensions of consciousness-purification: satya (truth-consciousness), tapas (concentration of consciousness-force), samyag-jñāna (integral knowledge), brahmacarya (consecration of being). 'Jyotir-maya' = supramental light — descended into the body.
aurobindo.ins: Four paths, one goal. Truth — not just not-lying but alignment with reality. Tapas — concentrated will. Right knowledge — not intellectual but integral, felt in every cell. Brahmacarya — consecrating your entire being to the divine. What you find is light within the body — the supramental consciousness, already there, waiting for your faults to clear.

dp.q: 🔍 The fourfold sādhana — truth, tapas, knowledge, brahmacarya
dp.a: This mantra prescribes four qualifications for attaining the Self — the most systematic sādhana statement in the Muṇḍaka: (1) Satya (truth): the moral dimension. Without truthfulness, spiritual practice is built on sand. Truth here means: (a) truthful speech — saying what is real, (b) truthful conduct — acting in alignment with reality, (c) truthful being — living without self-deception. The Chāndogya's Satyakāma is the model — his truthfulness WAS his qualification. (2) Tapas (austerity): the transformative dimension. Tapas = concentrated effort, self-discipline, the willingness to endure discomfort for growth. In the Muṇḍaka's vocabulary, tapas has appeared as both cosmic (Brahman's creative tapas) and personal (the aspirant's practice). (3) Samyag-jñāna (right knowledge): the cognitive dimension. Not just any knowledge but 'samyak' — correct, complete, direct. This is parā vidyā (higher knowledge) as defined in 1.1.5 — knowledge of 'that by which the imperishable is known.' Mere intellectual understanding or scriptural scholarship is aparā (lower). (4) Brahmacarya (self-discipline): the energetic dimension. Brahmacarya literally means 'conduct toward Brahman' — a life oriented toward the divine. It includes celibacy but is much broader: conservation of vital energy, restraint of the senses, living under a teacher's guidance, dedication of one's entire lifestyle to the goal. The fourfold integration: none of the four alone suffices. Truth without tapas lacks transformative power. Tapas without knowledge is blind. Knowledge without brahmacarya dissipates. All four must work together — moral purity (satya), concentrated effort (tapas), correct understanding (samyag-jñāna), and disciplined lifestyle (brahmacarya).

dp.q: 🔍 'Antaḥ-śarīre jyotir-mayaḥ' — the light within the body
dp.a: The phrase 'antaḥ-śarīre jyotir-mayaḥ' (within the body, made of light) places the Self not in a transcendent beyond but right here, inside the body: The implication: you don't need to travel to another world, reach a distant heaven, or transcend the body to find the Self. The Self is 'antaḥ-śarīre' — within the body. It's not brought from outside; it's already there, always has been, always will be. Why 'jyotir-maya' (made of light)? (1) Self-luminosity: the Self doesn't need external illumination — it IS light. The Kaṭha (2.2.15) makes this explicit: 'na tatra sūryo bhāti na candra-tārakam, nemā vidyuto bhānti kuto'yam agniḥ / tam eva bhāntam anubhāti sarvaṁ, tasya bhāsā sarvam idaṁ vibhāti' — 'There the sun doesn't shine, nor the moon, nor stars, nor lightning, much less fire. Everything shines after Him; by His light, all this is illumined.' (2) Consciousness = light: in the Upanishadic metaphor system, light (jyotis) = consciousness (cit). To say the Self is 'made of light' is to say it IS consciousness — pure, luminous, self-aware. (3) 'Śubhra' (pure/resplendent): the Self-light is not mixed with darkness — it is pure, brilliant, unstained. Even while dwelling within the body (with all its impurities), the Self remains śubhra. Who sees it? 'Yatayaḥ kṣīṇa-doṣāḥ' — ascetics/strivers whose faults are destroyed. The light is always there; the obstacle is our own inner impurities. Remove the faults (through the fourfold sādhana), and the light that was always shining becomes visible.

sk: सत्यमेव जयते नानृतं सत्येन पन्था विततो देवयानः येनाक्रमन्त्यृषयो ह्याप्तकामा यत्र तत्सत्यस्य परमं निधानम् ||
ro: satyam · eva · jayate · na · anṛtaṁ · satyena · panthāḥ · vitataḥ · deva-yānaḥ · yena · ākramanti · ṛṣayaḥ · hi · āpta-kāmāḥ · yatra · tat · satyasya · paramaṁ · nidhānam ||
hi: सत्यम् एव जयते (truth alone prevails / सत्य ही जीतता है) — न अनृतम् (not untruth / असत्य नहीं)। सत्येन (by truth / सत्य से) पन्थाः (the path / मार्ग) विततः (is spread out / विस्तृत) देवयानः (the path of the gods / देवयान-मार्ग) — येन (by which) ऋषयः (the sages) आप्तकामाः (whose desires are fulfilled / पूर्णकाम) आक्रमन्ति (ascend / journey / चढ़ते हैं) — यत्र (where) तत् सत्यस्य (of truth / सत्य का) परमं निधानम् (supreme treasure / परम निधान) [है]।
en: Truth alone prevails (satyam eva jayate), not untruth (na anṛtam). By truth (satyena) is spread out (vitataḥ) the path of the gods (deva-yānaḥ), by which the sages (ṛṣayaḥ), whose desires are fulfilled (āpta-kāmāḥ), ascend (ākramanti) — to where (yatra) is the supreme treasure (paramaṁ nidhānam) of truth (satyasya).

ws.h: सत्य ही जीतता है / truth alone prevails
ws.e: truth alone prevails — satyam (truth) + eva (alone/indeed) + jayate (conquers/prevails); the national motto of India; truth is not merely a value but the fundamental principle of reality — what is real ultimately prevails over what is unreal

ws.h: असत्य / untruth / falsehood
ws.e: untruth / falsehood — an + ṛta (cosmic order/truth); literally 'that which is against ṛta (the cosmic order)'; untruth is not merely a lie but a violation of the fundamental order of reality

ws.h: देवयान / the path of the gods / the luminous path
ws.e: the path of the gods — deva (gods/luminous beings) + yāna (path/vehicle); the 'northern path' through which the liberated soul travels to the highest Brahman; contrasted with pitṛ-yāna (path of the fathers) which leads to rebirth; cf. Chāndogya 5.10, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2

ws.h: पूर्णकाम / whose desires are fulfilled / desireless
ws.e: whose desires are fulfilled — āpta (attained/fulfilled) + kāma (desires); the sages have 'attained their desires' — not by satisfying every wish but by realising the Self which is the source of all satisfaction; they are pūrṇa-kāma (full in desire)

ws.h: परम निधान / supreme treasure / ultimate abode
ws.e: the supreme treasure / the ultimate repository — parama (supreme) + nidhāna (treasure/repository/abode); the final destination — where the highest truth is stored, where Brahman 'resides'; the ultimate goal of the path of truth

gr: 'Satyameva Jayate' — the most famous mantra of the Muṇḍaka: this is the single most widely known line from any Upanishad — it is the national motto of India, inscribed beneath the Lion Capital of Ashoka on the national emblem. The declaration: 'satyam eva jayate, na anṛtam' — 'truth alone prevails, not untruth.' This is not merely a moral exhortation — it is a metaphysical statement about the nature of reality. Truth (satya) = what is real, what actually exists. Untruth (anṛta) = what is unreal, what merely appears to exist. The mantra says: ultimately, reality prevails over appearance, being over seeming, the true over the false. The path: 'satyena panthāḥ vitataḥ deva-yānaḥ' — 'by truth is spread out the path of the gods.' The deva-yāna (path of the gods / luminous path) is the path of no-return — the path through which liberated souls travel to Brahman. This path is 'spread out' (vitata) BY truth — truth itself constructs the road. The travellers: 'ṛṣayaḥ āpta-kāmāḥ' — 'sages whose desires are fulfilled.' The ṛṣis who travel this path are 'āpta-kāma' — their desires are 'attained' / 'fulfilled.' This doesn't mean they got everything they wanted; it means they found the Self which is the source of all desire — and in that, all desire is fulfilled. The destination: 'yatra tat satyasya paramaṁ nidhānam' — 'where is the supreme treasure of truth.' The path of truth leads to the treasure-house of truth — Brahman, the ultimate reality.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.6 — This is the most culturally significant mantra in the entire Muṇḍaka — 'satyameva jayate' is the national motto of India, adopted in 1950 and inscribed on the national emblem (the Sarnath Lion Capital of Ashoka). The phrase appears in the Muṇḍaka alone among the Upanishads, though the concept pervades Vedic literature (cf. ṛta in the Ṛg Veda). The deva-yāna (path of the gods) is described in detail in the Chāndogya (5.10.1-2) and Bṛhadāraṇyaka (6.2.15): from flame → day → bright fortnight → six months of northern course → year → sun → moon → lightning → and finally to Brahman, guided by a non-human person (amānava puruṣa). Contrasted with the pitṛ-yāna (path of the fathers) — smoke → night → dark fortnight → six months of southern course → rebirth. The 'āpta-kāmāḥ' (those whose desires are fulfilled) echoes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.6): 'tasya dhīrāḥ parijānanti yonim' and the Taittirīya (2.1.1): 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma … sa āpta-kāma.' The phrase 'paramaṁ nidhānam' (supreme treasure) suggests Brahman as a hidden treasure — the pearl of great price.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'सत्यमेव जयते' = सत् (real / being) ही अन्ततः विजयी — असत् (unreal) = माया (illusion) = पराजित। यह नैतिक (ethical) और आध्यात्मिक (metaphysical) दोनों कथन है। 'देवयान' = ज्ञान-मार्ग (path of knowledge) — ब्रह्म-लोक तक। 'परमं निधानम्' = निर्गुण ब्रह्म (attributeless Brahman) — परम सत्य — जहाँ कोई लौटकर नहीं आता।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'satyameva jayate' = sat (the real/being) alone ultimately prevails — asat (the unreal) = māyā (illusion) = is defeated. This is both ethical and metaphysical. 'Deva-yāna' = the path of knowledge — to Brahma-loka. 'Paramaṁ nidhānam' = nirguṇa Brahman (attributeless Brahman) — the supreme truth — from which there is no return.
advaita.ins: Truth alone prevails. Not eventually — ultimately. The real outlasts the unreal, being outlasts seeming, consciousness outlasts ignorance. The path to Brahman is made of truth — laid out by truth, walked in truth, leading to the supreme treasure of truth. The sages who walk it need nothing — because they've found the Self, and in the Self, all desires are already fulfilled.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सत्यमेव जयते' = भगवान् (God) = सत्य (truth) — वही अन्ततः विजयी। 'देवयान' = भक्ति-मार्ग (path of devotion) — भगवत्-प्राप्ति (God-attainment) का मार्ग। 'परमं निधानम्' = भगवान् का दिव्य धाम (divine abode / Vaikuṇṭha) — जहाँ भक्त शाश्वत आनन्द (eternal bliss) भोगते हैं।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'satyameva jayate' = God = truth — He alone ultimately prevails. 'Deva-yāna' = the path of devotion — the path to God-attainment. 'Paramaṁ nidhānam' = the Lord's divine abode (Vaikuṇṭha) — where devotees enjoy eternal bliss.
vishisht.ins: Truth prevails — and God is truth. The path of the gods is the path of devotion — laid out by truth, walked in love, leading to God's own abode. The sages who walk it are fulfilled — not because they got everything they wanted, but because they found the One who IS everything they wanted.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'सत्यमेव जयते' = सत्य-चेतना (truth-consciousness) ही अन्ततः विजयी — असत्य = अज्ञान (ignorance) = चेतना का अवरोहण (involution)। 'देवयान' = चेतना-आरोहण (ascent of consciousness) — मनोमय (mental) से अतिमानसिक (supramental) तक। 'परमं निधानम्' = सच्चिदानन्द (sat-cit-ānanda) — सत्य का परम धाम।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'satyameva jayate' = truth-consciousness alone ultimately prevails — untruth = ignorance = the involution of consciousness. 'Deva-yāna' = the ascent of consciousness — from mental to supramental. 'Paramaṁ nidhānam' = sat-cit-ānanda — the supreme abode of truth.
aurobindo.ins: Truth alone prevails — because truth is the nature of consciousness, and consciousness is the nature of reality. The path of the gods is the path of consciousness ascending — from mind to overmind to supermind. The sages who walk it have fulfilled all desires not by satisfying them but by reaching the source — sat-cit-ānanda, the supreme treasure of truth.

dp.q: 🔍 'Satyameva Jayate' — from Upanishad to national motto
dp.a: The phrase 'satyameva jayate' has a remarkable history — from an esoteric Upanishadic teaching to the national motto of India: In the Muṇḍaka: the phrase occurs in the context of the final teaching on the path to Brahman. It is a metaphysical statement first and a moral statement second. 'Satya' here is not just honesty — it is 'that which is real' (sat = being). The mantra says: reality prevails over appearance, the true over the false. This is the nature of things — truth doesn't need to 'fight' to prevail; it prevails because it IS. The adoption: in 1950, the newly independent Republic of India adopted 'Satyameva Jayate' as its national motto. It was inscribed in Devanāgarī script beneath the Lion Capital of Ashoka (from Sarnath, 3rd century BCE), which became the national emblem. The political resonance: Mahatma Gandhi's philosophy of satyāgraha ('truth-force' / 'holding to truth') drew directly on this Upanishadic tradition. For Gandhi, truth was not merely a moral value but a cosmic force — the same force the Muṇḍaka describes. His conviction that non-violent truth would ultimately prevail over violent untruth echoed 'satyameva jayate, na anṛtam.' The philosophical depth: the phrase operates at multiple levels: (1) Ethical: truthful conduct prevails over deceit. (2) Metaphysical: sat (being/reality) prevails over asat (non-being/appearance). (3) Soteriological: the path of truth (satya → deva-yāna) leads to the supreme treasure, while the path of untruth leads to rebirth. (4) Cosmological: the universe is grounded in ṛta (cosmic order/truth) — disorder and falsehood are temporary deviations from the fundamental order.

dp.q: 🔍 The deva-yāna — the path of the gods
dp.a: The 'deva-yāna' (path of the gods / luminous path) is one of the most important concepts in Upanishadic soteriology: Two paths: the Upanishads describe two post-mortem paths: (1) Deva-yāna (path of the gods) — the path of no-return, leading to Brahman. Reserved for those who have knowledge (jñāna) or devotion (bhakti). (2) Pitṛ-yāna (path of the fathers) — the path of return, leading to the moon, then back to rebirth. For those who perform rituals without knowledge. The route (Chāndogya 5.10, Bṛhadāraṇyaka 6.2): flame → day → bright fortnight → six months of the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa) → the year → the sun → the moon → lightning → a non-human person (amānava puruṣa) who guides them to Brahman. What 'satyena vitataḥ' means: the path is 'spread out BY truth' — truth itself is the substance of the road. The deva-yāna is not a physical route through space but a path of increasing truth-realisation. Each 'station' (flame, sun, lightning) represents a stage of consciousness-ascent. 'Āpta-kāmāḥ' — whose desires are fulfilled: the travellers on this path are 'āpta-kāma' — their desires are 'attained.' The Taittirīya (2.1.1) says of the Brahman-knower: 'āpnoti sarvān kāmān saha brahmaṇā vipaścitā' — 'they attain all desires together with the omniscient Brahman.' This doesn't mean every worldly wish is granted — it means the Self is found, and in the Self is everything one could ever desire. 'Paramaṁ nidhānam' — 'the supreme treasure': the destination is not a place but a reality — the 'supreme repository of truth,' the ultimate Real. The metaphor of 'nidhāna' (treasure) suggests that truth is not merely an attribute of reality but IS reality — and it is inexhaustibly rich, like a treasure that never runs out.

sk: बृहच्च तद्दिव्यमचिन्त्यरूपं सूक्ष्मं च तत्सूक्ष्मतरं विभाति दूरात्सुदूरे तदिहान्तिके च पश्यत्स्विहैव निहितं गुहायाम् ||
ro: bṛhat · ca · tat · divyam · acintya-rūpaṁ · sūkṣmaṁ · ca · tat · sūkṣmataragm · vibhāti · dūrāt · sudūre · tat · iha · antike · ca · paśyatsu · iha · eva · nihitaṁ · guhāyām ||
hi: बृहत् (vast / विराट) और वह (तत्) दिव्यम् (divine / दिव्य), अचिन्त्यरूपम् (of unthinkable form / अचिन्तनीय रूप वाला), सूक्ष्म (subtle / सूक्ष्म) — और सूक्ष्मतरम् (subtler than the subtle / सूक्ष्म से भी सूक्ष्मतर) विभाति (shines / प्रकाशित होता है)। दूरात् सुदूरे (far beyond the far / दूर से भी अत्यन्त दूर) — तत् (that) इह (here) अन्तिके (near / समीप) च (and also)। पश्यत्सु (among those who see / देखने वालों में) इह एव (right here) निहितम् (placed / स्थित) गुहायाम् (in the cave [of the heart])।
en: Vast (bṛhat) is that (tat), divine (divyam), of unthinkable form (acintya-rūpam), subtle (sūkṣmam) — subtler than the subtle (sūkṣmataram) It shines (vibhāti). Far beyond the far (dūrāt sudūre), yet here (iha), near (antike) — among those who see (paśyatsu), It is placed (nihitam) right here (iha eva), in the cave of the heart (guhāyām).

ws.h: अचिन्तनीय रूप वाला / of unthinkable form
ws.e: of unthinkable form — a + cintya (thinkable) + rūpa (form); Brahman has 'form' but it cannot be grasped by the mind; it is beyond conception, not formless but trans-formal

ws.h: सूक्ष्म से भी सूक्ष्मतर / subtler than the subtle
ws.e: subtler than the subtle — comparative of sūkṣma; Brahman is more subtle than the subtlest thing conceivable; cf. Kaṭha 1.2.8: 'aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān' — 'smaller than the small, greater than the great'

ws.h: दूर से भी अत्यन्त दूर / far beyond the far
ws.e: far beyond the far — the superlative of distance; Brahman is more remote than anything distant; yet the next phrase says it is also 'antike' (near) — the paradox of the simultaneously transcendent and immanent

ws.h: गुहा में / हृदय-गुहा में / in the cave of the heart
ws.e: in the cave — guhā = cave; in the Upanishads, 'guhā' = the innermost chamber of the heart (hṛdaya), the 'cave' within which the Self is hidden; cf. Kaṭha 1.2.12: 'guhāhitaṁ gahvareṣṭhaṁ purāṇam'

gr: The paradox of Brahman — simultaneously vast and subtle, far and near: this mantra describes Brahman through a series of paradoxes — each pair of opposites showing that Brahman transcends all categories. The paradoxes: (1) Bṛhat + sūkṣma: vast AND subtle. Brahman is the largest (encompasses everything) and the smallest (pervades the atom). (2) Divya + nihitaṁ guhāyām: divine/transcendent AND hidden in the heart. Brahman is the most exalted reality and the most intimate presence. (3) Dūrāt sudūre + iha antike: far beyond the far AND right here, near. Brahman is more remote than the most distant star and closer than your own heartbeat. Acintya-rūpam — 'of unthinkable form': Brahman has 'form' (rūpa) but it is 'acintya' (unthinkable / beyond thought). This is not formlessness but trans-formality — a form that exceeds the mind's capacity to conceive. The Kaṭha parallel (1.2.21): 'āsīno dūraṁ vrajati, śayāno yāti sarvataḥ' — 'Sitting, It travels far; lying down, It goes everywhere.' The same paradox of stillness-in-motion, near-yet-far. The Īśā parallel (5): 'tad ejati tan naijati, tad dūre tad v antike, tad antar asya sarvasya, tad u sarvasyāsya bāhyataḥ' — 'It moves; It does not move. It is far; It is near. It is within all this; It is outside all this.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.7 — The paradoxical description of Brahman here closely parallels: (1) Kaṭha 1.2.20-21: 'aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān' + 'āsīno dūraṁ vrajati.' (2) Īśā 5: 'tad ejati tan naijati, tad dūre tad v antike.' (3) Śvetāśvatara 3.20: 'aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān ātmāsya jantoḥ nihito guhāyām.' The term 'acintya-rūpa' (unthinkable form) anticipates later Vaiṣṇava theology's use of 'acintya-bhedābheda' (inconceivable difference-and-non-difference). The 'guhā' (cave of the heart) motif is ubiquitous in the Upanishads: Kaṭha 1.2.12, 1.3.1, 2.3.17; Taittirīya 2.1; Chāndogya 8.1.1 (the 'daharavidyā' — meditation on the small space within the heart).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — सभी विरोधाभास (paradoxes) = ब्रह्म सभी द्वन्द्वों (dualities) से परे। 'बृहत्' = सर्वव्यापक। 'सूक्ष्म' = अविभाज्य (indivisible)। 'दूरात् सुदूरे' = अज्ञानी के लिए दूर। 'इह अन्तिके' = ज्ञानी के लिए निकट — हृदय-गुहा में। ब्रह्म = अज्ञानी के लिए सुदूर, ज्ञानी के लिए सुसमीप।
advaita.en: Shankara says all paradoxes = Brahman is beyond all dualities. 'Bṛhat' = all-pervading. 'Sūkṣma' = indivisible. 'Dūrāt sudūre' = far for the ignorant. 'Iha antike' = near for the wise — in the cave of the heart. Brahman = infinitely far for the ignorant, infinitely near for the wise.
advaita.ins: Every paradox points to the same truth — Brahman can't be caught in a single category. It's vast AND subtle, far AND near, divine AND hidden in your heart. The distance is only your ignorance. The nearness is what remains when ignorance is gone. It was always right here — in the cave of the heart.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'बृहत्' = भगवान् विराट (immense) — सम्पूर्ण विश्व उनका शरीर। 'सूक्ष्म' = भगवान् अणु (atomic) से भी सूक्ष्म — प्रत्येक जीव में अन्तर्यामी। 'गुहायाम्' = हृदय-कमल (lotus of the heart) में — भगवान् सदा विराजमान।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'bṛhat' = the Lord is immense — the entire universe is His body. 'Sūkṣma' = the Lord is subtler than the atom — the inner controller in every being. 'Guhāyām' = in the lotus of the heart — the Lord always resides.
vishisht.ins: God is vaster than the universe — and subtler than an atom. Farther than the farthest star — and closer than your own heart. He lives in the cave of the heart, waiting for you to look inward. The paradox isn't a puzzle — it's an invitation.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'बृहत्' = विश्व-चेतना (universal consciousness)। 'सूक्ष्म' = आणविक चेतना (atomic consciousness)। 'अचिन्त्यरूप' = अतिमानसिक (supramental) = मन (mind) की सीमा से परे। चेतना सभी स्तरों (levels) पर एक साथ विद्यमान — विराट से अणु तक, दूर से निकट तक।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'bṛhat' = universal consciousness. 'Sūkṣma' = atomic consciousness. 'Acintya-rūpa' = supramental = beyond the mind's limit. Consciousness exists simultaneously at all levels — from the vast to the atomic, from the far to the near.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is simultaneously everything — vast as the universe, subtle as a quantum, far as the farthest reaches of space, near as the cave of your heart. The 'unthinkable form' isn't formless — it's a form too vast for the mind. But the seers see it — right here, right now, in the innermost cave.

dp.q: 🔍 The paradoxes of Brahman — far and near, vast and subtle
dp.a: This mantra describes Brahman through paradoxes that appear throughout the Upanishads: (1) Bṛhat + sūkṣma (vast + subtle): the Kaṭha (1.2.20) says: 'aṇoḥ aṇīyān mahato mahīyān' — 'smaller than the smallest, greater than the greatest.' Brahman is simultaneously the largest thing (it encompasses everything — 'sarvam idaṁ brahma,' Chāndogya 3.14.1) and the smallest (it pervades the innermost atom — 'aṇu' in the Kaṭha). It is not one OR the other — it is BOTH. (2) Dūrāt sudūre + iha antike (far + near): the Īśā (5) captures this perfectly: 'tad dūre tad v antike' — 'It is far; It is near.' Brahman is 'far' because it transcends all mental categories — no amount of thinking, travelling, or searching will reach it if you look in the wrong direction. But it is 'near' — 'nihitaṁ guhāyām' (placed in the cave of the heart) — because it IS you, it is your innermost Self, closer than your breath. (3) Divya + guhā (divine + hidden): Brahman is 'divya' (divine/transcendent) — the most exalted reality. Yet it is 'nihitam guhāyām' — hidden/placed in the cave of the heart, the most intimate interior. Why paradoxes? Because Brahman is beyond the categories the mind uses to classify reality (big/small, far/near, inner/outer). Any single description would be misleading. Only paradoxes — holding opposites together — can point to what lies beyond both.

dp.q: 🔍 'Guhāyām' — the cave of the heart in the Upanishads
dp.a: The 'guhā' (cave) is one of the most powerful and recurring images in the Upanishads — the innermost chamber of the heart where the Self is hidden: Major guhā passages: (1) Kaṭha (1.2.12): 'guhā-hitaṁ gahvareṣṭhaṁ purāṇam' — 'The ancient one, hidden in the cave, dwelling in the abyss.' (2) Kaṭha (1.3.1): 'ṛtaṁ pibantau sukṛtasya loke guhāṁ praviṣṭau parame parārdhe' — 'The two [jīva and Brahman], drinking truth, having entered the cave, in the highest heaven.' (3) Taittirīya (2.1): Brahman is 'nihitam guhāyām' — placed in the cave. (4) Chāndogya (8.1.1): the 'dahara-vidyā' — 'In this city of Brahman [the body], there is a small lotus, a dwelling; within it, a small space (dahara ākāśa). What is within that — that should be sought.' What is the 'cave'? The guhā is not a physical cavity — it is the innermost core of consciousness, the space within the heart-centre where awareness turns upon itself. In meditation, the practitioner withdraws attention from the senses, from the mind, from the intellect, and enters the 'cave' — the space of pure awareness beyond thought. The teaching: the Self is not in a temple, on a mountaintop, or in a distant heaven. It is 'nihitaṁ guhāyām' — placed in the innermost cave of your own being. The journey to Brahman is an inward journey — from the surface of experience to the depth of being.

sk: न चक्षुषा गृह्यते नापि वाचा नान्यैर्देवैस्तपसा कर्मणा वा ज्ञानप्रसादेन विशुद्धसत्त्वस्ततस्तु तं पश्यते निष्कलं ध्यायमानः ||
ro: na · cakṣuṣā · gṛhyate · na · api · vācā · na · anyaiḥ · devaiḥ · tapasā · karmaṇā · vā · jñāna-prasādena · viśuddha-sattvaḥ · tataḥ · tu · taṁ · paśyate · niṣkalaṁ · dhyāyamānaḥ ||
hi: न चक्षुषा (not by the eye / आँख से नहीं) गृह्यते (is grasped / पकड़ा जाता), न वाचा (not by speech / वाणी से नहीं), न अन्यैः देवैः (not by other senses/gods / अन्य इन्द्रियों/देवों से नहीं), तपसा कर्मणा वा (nor by tapas or action / तप या कर्म से भी नहीं)। ज्ञानप्रसादेन (by the grace/clarity of knowledge / ज्ञान की प्रसन्नता/कृपा से) विशुद्धसत्त्वः (one whose sattva is purified / शुद्ध सत्त्व वाला) — ततः तु (then indeed) तम् (that / Him) पश्यते (sees / देखता है) निष्कलम् (the partless / निष्कल / without parts) ध्यायमानः (meditating / ध्यान करता हुआ)।
en: Not by the eye (na cakṣuṣā) is It grasped (gṛhyate), not by speech (na vācā), not by other senses/gods (na anyaiḥ devaiḥ), not by tapas or action (tapasā karmaṇā vā). By the grace/clarity of knowledge (jñāna-prasādena), one whose sattva is purified (viśuddha-sattva) — then (tataḥ tu) one sees (paśyate) that partless [Brahman] (niṣkalam), meditating (dhyāyamānaḥ).

ws.h: पकड़ा जाता है / is grasped / is seized
ws.e: is grasped / is seized — from √grah (to grasp/seize); the senses 'grasp' objects — but they cannot grasp Brahman; Brahman is not an object that can be grasped by any instrument of knowledge

ws.h: ज्ञान की प्रसन्नता/कृपा/निर्मलता से / by the grace/clarity of knowledge
ws.e: by the grace/clarity/serenity of knowledge — jñāna (knowledge) + prasāda (grace/clarity/serenity); prasāda has two intertwined meanings: (1) grace — knowledge is received, not manufactured; (2) clarity/serenity — the mind becomes clear, still, transparent, and the Self shines through

ws.h: शुद्ध सत्त्व वाला / one whose sattva is purified
ws.e: one whose sattva (being/essence/purity) is purified — vi + śuddha (thoroughly purified) + sattva (the quality of purity/clarity/goodness); the inner nature must be thoroughly cleansed for the Self to be seen

ws.h: निष्कल / अंश-रहित / partless / without parts
ws.e: partless / without divisions — niṣ (without) + kalā (part/division); Brahman has no parts, cannot be divided, cannot be broken into components; it is an absolute unity

gr: What cannot reach Brahman — and what can: this mantra follows a 'neti neti' (not this, not this) structure — first listing what CANNOT grasp Brahman, then revealing what CAN. What cannot: (1) cakṣus (eye) — sight cannot perceive Brahman; Brahman is not a visual object. (2) vāc (speech) — words cannot capture Brahman; language fails (cf. Taittirīya 2.9.1: 'yato vāco nivartante'). (3) anyaiḥ devaiḥ (other senses/gods) — hearing, touch, smell, taste — none of the sense-organs can reach Brahman. (4) tapas (austerity) — even tapas, the Muṇḍaka's central sādhana, is here declared insufficient BY ITSELF. (5) karma (action) — ritual action cannot reach the partless (niṣkala) Brahman. What CAN: 'jñāna-prasādena viśuddha-sattvaḥ' — 'by the grace/clarity of knowledge, one whose sattva is purified.' Two conditions: (a) inner purity (viśuddha-sattva) — the being must be cleansed of impurities; (b) the grace/clarity of knowledge (jñāna-prasāda) — a grace that descends when conditions are right. The word 'prasāda': carries both 'grace' and 'clarity' — suggesting that the seeing of Brahman is both a gift and a natural result of inner purification. The mind becomes still (prasanna), clear like undisturbed water, and the Self is reflected in it perfectly.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.8 — The structure of this mantra closely parallels the Kaṭha (1.2.23): 'nāyam ātmā pravacanena labhyaḥ, na medhayā na bahunā śrutena / yam evaiṣa vṛṇute tena labhyaḥ, tasyaiṣa ātmā vivṛṇute tanūṁ svām' — 'This Self is not attained by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing. He whom the Self chooses, by him is the Self attained — to him the Self reveals Its own form.' Both mantras combine negative theology (Brahman cannot be reached by X, Y, Z) with a positive statement involving grace/choice. The word 'prasāda' is multivalent: (1) 'grace' — the most common theological reading, especially in Vaiṣṇava traditions; (2) 'clarity/serenity' — the most common Advaitin reading (the mind becomes prasanna = clear/serene); (3) 'prasāda' as the consecrated offering returned to the devotee — the 'grace-gift' of the deity. The tension between 'prasāda' (grace/gift) and the fourfold sādhana of 3.2.5 (satya, tapas, samyag-jñāna, brahmacarya) is deliberate — both self-effort and grace are necessary.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'न चक्षुषा' = इन्द्रियाँ ब्रह्म तक नहीं पहुँचतीं — ब्रह्म = इन्द्रिय-विषय (sense-object) नहीं। 'ज्ञानप्रसादेन' = ज्ञान की निर्मलता (clarity of knowledge) — बुद्धि (intellect) शान्त (serene) होने पर, मन (mind) स्वच्छ (transparent) होने पर — आत्मा स्वयं प्रकट (self-reveals)। 'निष्कलम्' = निर्गुण ब्रह्म — अंश-रहित — ध्यान (meditation) में प्रकट।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'na cakṣuṣā' = the senses cannot reach Brahman — Brahman is not a sense-object. 'Jñāna-prasādena' = the clarity of knowledge — when the intellect is serene, when the mind is transparent — the Self self-reveals. 'Niṣkalam' = nirguṇa Brahman — without parts — revealed in meditation.
advaita.ins: You can't see Brahman with your eyes, speak it with your words, or reach it with rituals and austerities. Then how? By the clarity of knowledge — when your mind becomes utterly still, utterly pure, like clear water. Then the partless Self reveals itself. Not because you grasped it — because you stopped grasping.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'ज्ञानप्रसादेन' = भगवत्-कृपा (God's grace) + ज्ञान (knowledge)। भगवान् = कृपा से प्राप्त — केवल स्व-प्रयत्न (self-effort) से नहीं। 'विशुद्धसत्त्वः' = शुद्ध हृदय = भक्ति (devotion) का फल। भगवान् स्वयं भक्त को दर्शन देते हैं (God reveals Himself to the devotee)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'jñāna-prasādena' = God's grace + knowledge. God is attained by grace — not by self-effort alone. 'Viśuddha-sattva' = pure heart = the fruit of devotion. God Himself reveals Himself to the devotee.
vishisht.ins: Eyes can't see God. Words can't describe Him. Even tapas and ritual can't reach Him alone. Then how? By the grace of knowledge — God reveals Himself when your heart is pure. It's not your effort that brings the vision — it's His grace responding to your purity.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — इन्द्रियाँ (senses) = मानसिक चेतना (mental consciousness) — ब्रह्म तक नहीं पहुँचतीं। 'ज्ञानप्रसाद' = चेतना का उच्चतर स्तर (higher level of consciousness) — अतिमानसिक प्रज्ञा (supramental gnosis) — जो मन से परे है। 'विशुद्धसत्त्व' = अन्तर-शुद्धि (inner purification) — चेतना-रूपान्तर (consciousness-transformation) का पूर्वापेक्ष (prerequisite)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says senses = mental consciousness — cannot reach Brahman. 'Jñāna-prasāda' = a higher level of consciousness — supramental gnosis — beyond the mind. 'Viśuddha-sattva' = inner purification — the prerequisite for consciousness-transformation.
aurobindo.ins: The senses are instruments of the mind — they can't reach what is beyond the mind. Neither can tapas or action alone. What reaches Brahman is a higher consciousness — the gnosis that descends when the inner being is purified. It's not effort that produces the vision — it's the clearing of obstacles so that the light, which is always there, can enter.

dp.q: 🔍 'Jñāna-prasāda' — the debate between effort and grace
dp.a: The term 'jñāna-prasāda' is one of the most debated in the Muṇḍaka — it sits at the intersection of the age-old tension between self-effort and divine grace: The effort side: mantra 3.2.5 just prescribed FOUR sādhanas — satya, tapas, samyag-jñāna, brahmacarya. These are clearly human efforts — things the aspirant does. And the aspirant must be 'viśuddha-sattva' (purified in being) — which requires sustained practice. The grace side: this mantra (3.2.8) says that NONE of the instruments of effort — senses, speech, tapas, karma — can 'grasp' Brahman. Only 'jñāna-prasāda' can. The word 'prasāda' means grace/gift/serenity — suggesting something received, not produced. The Kaṭha parallel (1.2.23) makes the grace dimension explicit: 'yam evaiṣa vṛṇute tena labhyaḥ' — 'He whom the Self CHOOSES, by him is the Self attained — to him the Self reveals Its own form.' The Self chooses and reveals — the aspirant does not seize it. The resolution: most commentators agree that BOTH are necessary: (1) Self-effort (the fourfold sādhana) prepares the ground — it purifies the sattva, removes obstacles, creates the conditions. (2) Grace/clarity (prasāda) is the actual moment of seeing — it descends when conditions are right, but it cannot be manufactured. It is like lighting a lamp in a clean room — you must clean the room (effort), but the light illumines on its own (grace). The practical implication: do the work (satya, tapas, jñāna, brahmacarya) — but don't imagine that the work itself produces the result. The result is a revelation — the Self reveals itself when you are ready. Your job is to be ready.

dp.q: 🔍 'Niṣkalam' — the partless Brahman
dp.a: The word 'niṣkalam' (partless / without divisions) describes the nature of Brahman as seen in the ultimate vision: What does 'partless' mean? (1) No spatial parts: Brahman doesn't have a top and a bottom, a left and a right, an inside and an outside. It cannot be divided in space. (2) No temporal parts: Brahman doesn't have a beginning, a middle, and an end. It cannot be divided in time. (3) No qualitative parts: Brahman is not composed of different qualities or attributes that could be separated. It is a simple, undifferentiated unity. Niṣkala vs. sakala: the Upanishads distinguish between: (a) Sakala Brahman (Brahman with parts) — Brahman as manifested in the world, with names, forms, and qualities. This is Brahman as seen through the lens of māyā/avidyā. (b) Niṣkala Brahman (Brahman without parts) — Brahman as it is in itself, beyond all differentiation. This is the ultimate reality. The meditative experience: 'niṣkalaṁ dhyāyamānaḥ' — 'meditating on the partless.' In deep meditation, all distinctions dissolve — subject and object, knower and known, self and world. What remains is a partless, undivided awareness — 'niṣkala.' This is not an absence (nothing left) but a presence (everything unified). The Śvetāśvatara (6.19): 'niṣkalaṁ niṣkriyaṁ śāntam — avadyaṁ nirañjanam' — 'Partless, actionless, peaceful — faultless, stainless.' The niṣkala Brahman is also niṣkriya (actionless), śānta (peaceful), niravadya (faultless), and nirañjana (stainless) — a cluster of negative descriptions pointing to a reality beyond all limitation.

sk: एषोऽणुरात्मा चेतसा वेदितव्यो यस्मिन्प्राणः पञ्चधा संविवेश चित्तं प्रजानां सर्वमोतं प्रोतं यस्मिन्विशुद्धे विभवत्येष आत्मा ||
ro: eṣaḥ · aṇuḥ · ātmā · cetasā · veditavyaḥ · yasmin · prāṇaḥ · pañcadhā · saṁviveśa · cittaṁ · prajānāṁ · sarvam · otaṁ · protaṁ · yasmin · viśuddhe · vibhavati · eṣaḥ · ātmā ||
hi: यह (एषः) अणु (subtle / atomic / सूक्ष्म) आत्मा (Self) चेतसा (by the mind/consciousness / चित्त/बुद्धि से) वेदितव्यः (is to be known / जानने योग्य) है — जिसमें (यस्मिन्) प्राण पञ्चधा (fivefold / पाँच प्रकार से) संविवेश (has entered / प्रविष्ट हुआ है)। प्रजानाम् (of beings / प्राणियों का) सर्वम् चित्तम् (all mind/consciousness) ओतं प्रोतम् (woven warp and weft / ताने-बाने की तरह बुना हुआ) — जिसमें (यस्मिन्) विशुद्धे (when purified / शुद्ध होने पर) विभवति (manifests / प्रकट होता है) यह (एषः) आत्मा (Self)।
en: This subtle (aṇu) Self (ātmā) is to be known (veditavyaḥ) by the mind/consciousness (cetasā) — in which (yasmin) prāṇa has entered (saṁviveśa) fivefold (pañcadhā). The mind/consciousness (citta) of all beings (prajānām) is woven warp and weft (otaṁ protam) [in the Self] — when that [mind] is purified (viśuddhe), this Self (eṣa ātmā) manifests (vibhavati).

ws.h: सूक्ष्म / atomic / subtle
