ws.e: subtle / atomic — aṇu = the smallest conceivable thing; the Self is aṇu not because it is literally atomic but because it is subtler than all physical and mental phenomena; it slips through every net of the senses

ws.h: पाँच प्रकार से / fivefold
ws.e: fivefold — the five prāṇas: prāṇa (outbreath), apāna (inbreath), vyāna (diffused breath), udāna (ascending breath), samāna (equalising breath); all five are 'woven into' the Self

ws.h: ताने-बाने में बुना हुआ / woven warp and weft
ws.e: woven in the warp and the weft — ota (woven lengthwise / warp) + prota (woven crosswise / weft); the Self pervades consciousness like threads pervade a cloth — horizontally and vertically, in every direction

ws.h: प्रकट होता है / manifests / becomes evident
ws.e: manifests / becomes evident — vi + √bhū (to become); the Self 'comes into manifestation' — not that it was absent, but that it becomes visible when the obstacles (impurities of citta) are removed

gr: The Self as the warp and weft of consciousness: this mantra uses a powerful weaving metaphor — the Self is 'otaṁ protam' (woven warp and weft) through the consciousness of all beings. 'Cetasā veditavyaḥ' — 'to be known by the mind': after the previous mantra said 'na cakṣuṣā gṛhyate' (not grasped by the eye), this mantra specifies the instrument — the 'cetas' (mind/consciousness/heart-mind). Not the outward-directed sensory mind but the purified, inward-turned awareness. 'Prāṇaḥ pañcadhā saṁviveśa' — 'prāṇa has entered fivefold': the five prāṇas (prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna) all function WITHIN the Self — the Self is the ground of all vital activity. 'Otaṁ protam' — the weaving metaphor: the Self pervades consciousness like threads pervade a cloth. You cannot find a part of the cloth that is without thread — similarly, you cannot find a moment of consciousness without the Self. The Self IS the fabric of awareness. 'Yasmin viśuddhe vibhavati' — 'when purified, the Self manifests': the key practical teaching — the Self is always present (otaṁ protam — woven through everything) but becomes manifest (vibhavati) only when the citta (mind) is purified (viśuddhe). The impurities of the mind are the only obstacle — remove them, and the Self that was always there shines forth.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.9 — The 'otaṁ protam' (woven warp and weft) metaphor also appears in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.8.7): Gārgī asks Yājñavalkya, 'What is that on which space itself is woven, warp and weft (otaṁ ca protaṁ ca)?' Answer: 'That, O Gārgī, the knowers of Brahman call the Imperishable (akṣara).' The fivefold prāṇa classification is standard in the Upanishads — cf. Praśna 3.5-7, where Pippalāda describes the five prāṇas in detail. The condition 'yasmin viśuddhe vibhavati' (when purified, the Self manifests) echoes the Yoga tradition — Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra 1.2: 'yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ' (yoga is the cessation of mental fluctuations) — when fluctuations cease (= citta is purified), the seer abides in its own nature (1.3).

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'चेतसा वेदितव्यः' = शुद्ध बुद्धि (purified intellect) से ज्ञेय। 'ओतं प्रोतम्' = आत्मा = सम्पूर्ण चेतना (all consciousness) का अधिष्ठान (substratum) — ताना-बाना। 'विशुद्धे विभवति' = चित्त-शुद्धि (citta-purification) से आत्मा प्रकट — आत्मा सदा विद्यमान (always present) — किन्तु अशुद्धि (impurity) आवरण (covering) है।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'cetasā veditavyaḥ' = to be known by the purified intellect. 'Otaṁ protam' = the Self = the substratum of all consciousness — warp and weft. 'Viśuddhe vibhavati' = through citta-purification, the Self manifests — the Self is always present but impurity is the covering.
advaita.ins: The Self is woven through your entire consciousness — every thought, every breath, every moment. Like thread in cloth, you can't separate it out. You can only see it by purifying the mind. When the mind is clear — the Self that was always there finally shows itself.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'अणुः आत्मा' = जीवात्मा = अणु-स्वरूप (atomic in nature) — भगवान् में अंश (part/mode of God)। 'ओतं प्रोतम्' = भगवान् = सम्पूर्ण चेतना में व्याप्त — अन्तर्यामी। 'विशुद्धे विभवति' = भक्ति-शुद्ध हृदय (devotion-purified heart) में भगवान् प्रकट।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'aṇuḥ ātmā' = the individual Self = atomic in nature — a part/mode of God. 'Otaṁ protam' = God pervades all consciousness — as the inner controller. 'Viśuddhe vibhavati' = God manifests in the devotion-purified heart.
vishisht.ins: God is woven through the consciousness of every being — warp and weft, inseparable from awareness itself. He's in every breath, every thought. Purify your heart through devotion, and He manifests — not from outside but from within, where He's always been.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'ओतं प्रोतम्' = चेतना (consciousness) = आत्मा (Self) का ताना-बाना। मन, प्राण, शरीर — सब चेतना से बुने हुए। 'विशुद्धे विभवति' = चेतना-शुद्धि (consciousness-purification) से आत्मा प्रकट — योग = चेतना-शुद्धि की प्रक्रिया।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'otaṁ protam' = consciousness = the warp and weft of the Self. Mind, prāṇa, body — all woven from consciousness. 'Viśuddhe vibhavati' = through consciousness-purification, the Self manifests — yoga = the process of consciousness-purification.
aurobindo.ins: Consciousness is not contained in the body — the body is contained in consciousness. The Self is woven through all awareness — mind, life, body — as thread through cloth. Purify consciousness, and the Self that was always the fabric of your being reveals itself. The thread was never hidden — your eyes were clouded.

dp.q: 🔍 'Otaṁ protam' — the weaving metaphor for Self and consciousness
dp.a: The image of 'otaṁ protam' (woven warp and weft) is one of the most vivid and philosophically significant metaphors in the Upanishads: The metaphor: in weaving, the warp (ota) consists of the lengthwise threads stretched on the loom, and the weft (prota) consists of the crosswise threads woven through them. Together, they create the fabric. The Muṇḍaka says: the Self is woven through consciousness like thread through cloth — in BOTH directions, at every point, inseparable from the fabric. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka version (3.8.7-8): Gārgī asks Yājñavalkya one of the most searching questions in all Upanishadic dialogue: 'In what is space itself woven, warp and weft?' Yājñavalkya answers: 'In the akṣara (the Imperishable), O Gārgī — that is the warp and weft of space itself.' What the metaphor teaches: (1) Pervasiveness: you cannot find a part of the cloth that is without thread. Similarly, you cannot find a moment of consciousness without the Self. (2) Intimacy: the Self is not 'in' consciousness the way a stone is in a bowl — it IS consciousness, the very substance from which awareness is made. (3) Inseparability: you cannot remove the thread without destroying the cloth. Similarly, the Self cannot be separated from consciousness — it IS what consciousness is. (4) Hiddenness: thread in a finished cloth is not immediately visible as individual threads — you see the pattern, the colour, the design, but not the individual threads. Similarly, the Self is 'hidden' in consciousness — present but not immediately obvious.

dp.q: 🔍 'Yasmin viśuddhe vibhavati' — purification as the key to Self-realisation
dp.a: The phrase 'yasmin viśuddhe vibhavati eṣa ātmā' ('when that [mind] is purified, this Self manifests') gives the Muṇḍaka's final practical instruction: The logic: (1) The Self is already present — it is 'otaṁ protam' (woven through all consciousness). It was never absent, never distant, never hidden. (2) The Self is not perceived because the citta (mind/consciousness) is aśuddha (impure) — clouded by desire, aversion, delusion, pride, and other doṣas (faults). (3) When the citta becomes viśuddha (thoroughly purified), the Self 'vibhavati' (manifests) — not because it arrives from elsewhere but because the covering is removed. The analogy: a mirror covered with dust doesn't reflect. The mirror is fine; the reflective surface is intact. The problem is the dust. Clean the dust, and the mirror reflects perfectly. Similarly, the Self is always 'reflecting' — but the impurities of the mind prevent the reflection from being seen. How to purify? The Muṇḍaka has answered this progressively: (1) The fourfold sādhana (3.2.5): satya, tapas, samyag-jñāna, brahmacarya. (2) The grace of knowledge (3.2.8): jñāna-prasāda. (3) Meditation on the partless (3.2.8): dhyāyamānaḥ niṣkalam. All three work together — ethical practice, intellectual clarity, and meditative absorption — to purify the citta and allow the ever-present Self to shine forth. The Yoga Sūtra parallel (1.2-3): Patañjali's formulation is virtually identical: 'yogaś citta-vṛtti-nirodhaḥ' (yoga = the cessation of mental fluctuations). 'Tadā draṣṭuḥ svarūpe'vasthānam' (then the seer abides in its own nature). When the mental fluctuations (vṛttis) cease — i.e., when the citta is purified — the seer (draṣṭṛ = the witness-Self) 'abides in its own form.' The same teaching, the same logic.

sk: यं यं लोकं मनसा संविभाति विशुद्धसत्त्वः कामयते यांश्च कामान् तं तं लोकं जयते तांश्च कामांस्तस्मादात्मज्ञं ह्यर्चयेद्भूतिकामः ||
ro: yaṁ · yaṁ · lokaṁ · manasā · saṁvibhāti · viśuddha-sattvaḥ · kāmayate · yāṁś · ca · kāmān · taṁ · taṁ · lokaṁ · jayate · tāṁś · ca · kāmān · tasmāt · ātma-jñaṁ · hi · arcayet · bhūti-kāmaḥ ||
en: Whatever world (yaṁ yaṁ lokam) [the knower] of purified sattva (viśuddha-sattva) envisions (saṁvibhāti) with the mind (manasā), and whatever desires (yāṁś ca kāmān) he desires (kāmayate) — that world (taṁ taṁ lokam) he wins (jayate), and those desires (tāṁś ca kāmān) [he fulfils]. Therefore (tasmāt), one who desires prosperity (bhūti-kāma) should worship (arcayet) the knower of the Self (ātma-jñam).
hi: जिस-जिस (यं-यं) लोक (world) को विशुद्धसत्त्व (purified being / शुद्ध सत्त्व वाला) मनसा (by mind / मन से) संविभाति (envisions / contemplates) और जिन-जिन कामों (desires) को कामयते (desires / चाहता है) — उन-उन लोकों को जयते (wins / जीत लेता है), और उन कामों को [पूर्ण करता है]। इसलिए (तस्मात्) भूतिकामः (one who desires prosperity / ऐश्वर्य चाहने वाला) आत्मज्ञम् (the knower of the Self / आत्मज्ञानी) को अर्चयेत् (should worship / should honour / पूजे)।

ws.h: मन से देखता है / envisions / contemplates
ws.e: envisions / illumines with the mind — saṁ + vi + √bhā (to shine); the purified mind doesn't merely 'think of' a world — it 'illumines' it, 'makes it shine'; the creative power of the purified mind

ws.h: शुद्ध सत्त्व वाला / one of purified being
ws.e: one whose being/essence is purified — this is the same qualification from 3.2.8; the purified knower's mind has creative power — what it envisions, becomes

ws.h: ऐश्वर्य चाहने वाला / one who desires prosperity
ws.e: one who desires prosperity/power/well-being — bhūti (prosperity/glory/becoming) + kāma (desire); the worldly person who wants success — even they should honour the knower of the Self

ws.h: पूजा करे / should worship / should honour
ws.e: should worship / honour / venerate — from √arc (to worship/praise); the instruction to worship the ātma-jña (Self-knower) — placing the sage above the priest, the king, and the ritual expert

gr: The creative power of the purified mind and the closing instruction: this mantra makes two bold claims: (1) The purified knower's mind is creative: whatever world the viśuddha-sattva envisions, he attains; whatever he desires, he fulfils. This is not wish-fulfilment or magical thinking — it is the natural power of a mind that is in alignment with reality (satya). The purified mind doesn't fantasise; it sees what is real, and what is real naturally comes to it. (2) The ātma-jña (Self-knower) should be worshipped: the mantra directly tells 'bhūti-kāmāḥ' (those who desire worldly prosperity) to worship the ātma-jña — the sage who knows the Self. This reverses the social hierarchy — normally kings and priests are honoured; here, the knower of the Self is placed above all. The practical implication: even if you don't seek liberation — even if you only want worldly success (bhūti) — your best course is to honour and serve the ātma-jña. The knower's blessings are more powerful than any ritual, any austerity, any worldly authority. This is the Muṇḍaka's closing teaching to the worldly audience — it bridges the gap between the spiritual and the practical, telling the worldly person: 'At least honour the sage — even your worldly goals will be furthered.'
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.10 — This mantra has close parallels in the Chāndogya (8.1.5-6): 'If he desires the world of the fathers, by his mere will the fathers come … whatever he desires, by his mere will it comes.' The creative power of the purified mind (saṅkalpa-śakti) is a recurring Upanishadic theme. The instruction to worship the ātma-jña echoes the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (3.9.26): the sage Yājñavalkya is venerated above the king. The Taittirīya (1.11.2) instructs the departing student: 'ācārya-devo bhava' — 'let the teacher be your god.' The phrase 'bhūti-kāma' (desirer of prosperity) pragmatically addresses those not yet ready for mokṣa — even they benefit from contact with the Self-knower. This is the Upanishad's concession to the world — not everyone seeks liberation, but everyone can benefit from the sage's presence.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'विशुद्धसत्त्वः' = ज्ञानी का मन (mind) = सत्य (truth) के अनुरूप — अतः उसका संकल्प (will) फलित होता है। 'आत्मज्ञं अर्चयेत्' = आत्मज्ञानी = सर्वोच्च (supreme) — मोक्ष न चाहने वाले भी उनका आदर करें — क्योंकि उनका सान्निध्य (proximity) = कल्याणकारी।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'viśuddha-sattva' = the knower's mind = aligned with truth — hence their will is effective. 'Ātma-jñaṁ arcayet' = the Self-knower = supreme — even those who don't seek mokṣa should honour them — because their proximity is beneficial.
advaita.ins: The sage's mind is aligned with reality — what they envision, happens. Not magic — alignment. Truth itself supports their will. Even if you only want worldly success, honour the sage. Their presence transforms you — not because of any ritual, but because of what they are.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'विशुद्धसत्त्वः' = भगवद्-भक्त (God-devotee) — जिसका हृदय शुद्ध — उसकी प्रार्थना (prayer) फलित (fruitful)। 'आत्मज्ञं अर्चयेत्' = भक्त-सेवा (serving the devotee) = भगवद्-सेवा (serving God) — क्योंकि भक्त = भगवान् का प्रतिनिधि (representative of God)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'viśuddha-sattva' = the God-devotee — whose heart is pure — their prayer is fruitful. 'Ātma-jñaṁ arcayet' = serving the devotee = serving God — because the devotee is God's representative.
vishisht.ins: The pure devotee's prayers are answered — not because of magical powers but because God honours the devotee's will. If you want prosperity, serve the devotee. Serving God's beloved is serving God Himself.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'संविभाति' = शुद्ध चेतना (purified consciousness) = सृजनात्मक (creative)। चेतना = शक्ति (force) — शुद्ध चेतना का संकल्प (will) = सत्य-शक्ति (truth-force) — जो वास्तविकता (reality) को आकार देती है। 'आत्मज्ञं अर्चयेत्' = चेतना-विकास (consciousness-evolution) में आत्मज्ञानी = अग्रदूत (pioneer)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'saṁvibhāti' = purified consciousness = creative. Consciousness = force — purified consciousness's will = truth-force — which shapes reality. 'Ātma-jñaṁ arcayet' = in consciousness-evolution, the Self-knower = the pioneer.
aurobindo.ins: Purified consciousness is creative. What the sage envisions becomes real — not through desire but through truth-force. If you want prosperity, approach the one whose consciousness is purified — the one who knows the Self. Their very presence realigns your consciousness with truth.

dp.q: 🔍 The creative power of the purified mind (saṅkalpa-śakti)
dp.a: This mantra ascribes creative power to the purified mind of the Self-knower — 'whatever world he envisions, he wins; whatever he desires, he fulfils': What is this power? (1) Not magical thinking: the mantra doesn't describe wish-fulfilment or supernatural powers (though later traditions read it this way). It describes the natural consequence of a mind aligned with satya (truth/reality). When the mind is viśuddha (purified), its perceptions and intentions are in harmony with the way things actually are — and actions born from such a mind naturally succeed. (2) Saṅkalpa-śakti (the power of resolve): in the Chāndogya (7.4.1), Sanatkumāra teaches: 'saṅkalpo vai manaḥ' — 'resolve is the essence of mind.' The mind's deepest power is its capacity to intend — to direct consciousness toward a goal. When the mind is pure, this power is undistorted and effective. (3) Alignment with ṛta: the Vedic concept of ṛta (cosmic order/truth) means that reality has an inherent order. A purified mind is aligned with this order — its desires are not random or selfish but in harmony with the cosmic flow. Such desires naturally fulfil themselves because they swim with the current of reality, not against it. The practical teaching for 'bhūti-kāmāḥ': even if you seek worldly prosperity, the sage is your best resource — not because the sage can magically grant wishes, but because proximity to a purified consciousness transforms your own consciousness. The sage's clarity, truthfulness, and alignment with reality become contagious.

dp.q: 🔍 'Ātma-jñaṁ arcayet' — why worship the Self-knower?
dp.a: The instruction 'ātma-jñaṁ arcayet' (worship the knower of the Self) is the Muṇḍaka's closing social teaching: The reversal of hierarchy: in Vedic society, the most honoured figures were kings (kṣatriyas) and priests (brāhmaṇas who perform rituals). The Muṇḍaka places the ātma-jña — the sage who knows the Self — above both. The Self-knower may not be a priest, may not perform rituals, may not hold any social rank — but they are to be worshipped. This is a radical statement of spiritual over social authority. Why worship the sage? (1) Transformative presence: the sage's presence purifies those around them — like a fire that warms everything nearby. Contact with a Self-knower accelerates the seeker's own development. (2) Teaching by being: the sage teaches not primarily through words (na ativādī — 3.1.4) but through being. Their state of ātma-krīḍa (playing in the Self) and ātma-rati (delighting in the Self) is itself the teaching. (3) The bridge for the worldly: for 'bhūti-kāmāḥ' (those who desire prosperity), the sage is the bridge between worldly aspiration and spiritual transformation. Even if one comes to the sage for worldly blessings, one receives spiritual upliftment. The Upanishadic tradition of guru-bhakti: this instruction connects to the guru-śiṣya (teacher-student) tradition that runs through all the Upanishads. The Taittirīya (1.11.2): 'ācārya-devo bhava' — let the teacher be your god. The Kaṭha (1.2.8-9): Nachiketa approaches Yama as a student approaches a teacher. The Muṇḍaka (1.2.12): 'tad-vijñānārthaṁ sa gurum evābhigacchet' — 'for the knowledge of That, one should approach a guru.' The closing verse of the Muṇḍaka now completes the circle — the student who approaches the guru ultimately becomes an ātma-jña worthy of worship by others.

sk: स वेदैतत्परमं ब्रह्म धाम यत्र विश्वं निहितं भाति शुभ्रम् उपासते पुरुषं ये ह्यकामास्ते शुक्रमेतदतिवर्तन्ति धीराः ||
ro: saḥ · veda · etat · paramaṁ · brahma · dhāma · yatra · viśvaṁ · nihitaṁ · bhāti · śubhram · upāsate · puruṣaṁ · ye · hi · akāmāḥ · te · śukram · etat · ativartanti · dhīrāḥ ||
hi: वह (सः) जानता है (वेद) इस (एतत्) परम ब्रह्म-धाम (supreme abode of Brahman / ब्रह्म के परम निवास) को — जहाँ (यत्र) विश्व (the universe) निहितम् (is placed / स्थित) है, भाति (shines / प्रकाशित होता है) शुभ्रम् (resplendent / शुद्ध)। जो (ये) अकामाः (desireless / निष्काम) पुरुष (the Person) को उपासते (worship / उपासना करते हैं) — वे (ते) धीराः (the wise / steady / धीर) शुक्रम् एतत् (this seed / luminous principle / बीज-तत्त्व) अतिवर्तन्ति (transcend / pass beyond / अतिक्रमण करते हैं)।
en: He knows (veda) this (etat) supreme abode of Brahman (paramaṁ brahma-dhāma), where (yatra) the universe (viśvam) is placed (nihitam), shining (bhāti) resplendent (śubhram). Those (ye) who are desireless (akāmāḥ) [and] worship (upāsate) the Person (puruṣam) — they (te), the wise (dhīrāḥ), transcend (ativartanti) this luminous seed (śukram etat).

ws.h: ब्रह्म का धाम / supreme abode of Brahman
ws.e: the supreme abode/dwelling of Brahman — brahma + dhāman (abode/seat/splendour); the 'place' where Brahman 'resides' — not a physical location but the ground of all existence; the universe itself is 'placed' within it

ws.h: शुद्ध / उज्ज्वल / resplendent / pure
ws.e: resplendent / pure / brilliant — from √śubh (to shine/be beautiful); the universe shines with Brahman's own radiance — it is not dark or inert but luminous with the light of consciousness

ws.h: निष्काम / desireless
ws.e: desireless — a + kāma (desire); not 'suppression of desire' but 'fulfilment beyond desire' — the ātma-jña is 'āpta-kāma' (desires fulfilled) and therefore 'akāma' (without remaining desire)

ws.h: बीज / तेज / seed / luminous substance
ws.e: the seed / luminous essence / generative principle — śukra = seed, bright substance; here = the seminal/creative force; the wise transcend (ativartanti) this — they go beyond the cycle of birth and generation

ws.h: धीर / स्थिर / wise / steady / resolute
ws.e: the wise / the steady / the resolute — from √dhī (to think/perceive) or dhīra (firm/courageous); the wise are those who see steadily and are not shaken by desire or fear

gr: The Muṇḍaka's closing seal: this is the final mantra of the entire Muṇḍaka Upanishad — it serves as the closing benediction and summary. 'Paramaṁ brahma-dhāma' — 'the supreme abode of Brahman': the knower knows THIS — the place where the entire universe is 'placed' (nihitam), shining resplendent (bhāti śubhram). This is not a location but a state of consciousness — the realisation that the universe rests in Brahman, shining with Brahman's light. 'Ye akāmāḥ puruṣaṁ upāsate' — 'those who are desireless and worship the Person': the final condition for liberation — akāma (desireless). Not desire-suppression but desire-transcendence — the wise have found the Self, and in the Self, all desire is fulfilled. They worship the Puruṣa (the Person / Brahman) — through meditation, knowledge, and devotion. 'Śukram etat ativartanti' — 'they transcend this luminous seed': the wise go beyond the cycle of birth and generation. 'Śukra' (seed / generative principle) represents the creative force that perpetuates saṁsāra — by transcending it, the wise escape the cycle of rebirth entirely. The closing word — 'dhīrāḥ': the Upanishad's final word is 'dhīrāḥ' — 'the wise / the steady.' The Muṇḍaka's entire teaching — from the two kinds of knowledge, through the fire-rituals, the bow-and-arrow meditation, the two birds, 'satyameva jayate,' to this final verse — is addressed to and culminates in the dhīra — the one who is wise, steady, resolute, and courageous enough to seek the truth.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: mundaka_upanishad_3.2.11 — This closing verse has near-exact parallels in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.8-10) and the Kaṭha (1.2.11, 2.3.14). The phrase 'paramaṁ brahma-dhāma' also appears in the Gītā (10.12): Arjuna says to Kṛṣṇa: 'paraṁ brahma paraṁ dhāma pavitraṁ paramaṁ bhavān' — 'You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the supreme purifier.' The word 'śukra' (seed/luminous substance) is significant — by transcending the 'seed,' the wise escape the very principle of generation/creation that perpetuates saṁsāra. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (4.4.6) describes the same idea: 'tad eva brahma tvaṁ viddhi, nedam yad idam upāsate' — 'Know that Brahman, not this [world] that people worship.' The Muṇḍaka ends where it began — with the distinction between higher and lower knowledge, now resolved: the wise (dhīrāḥ) know the supreme abode, worship the Person, and transcend the cycle of birth.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'परमं ब्रह्मधाम' = निर्गुण ब्रह्म = सर्वाधार (substratum of all)। 'विश्वं निहितम्' = विश्व = ब्रह्म में स्थित — ब्रह्म विश्व में नहीं। 'अकामाः' = निष्काम ज्ञानी — इच्छा-मुक्त। 'शुक्रम् अतिवर्तन्ति' = जन्म-मरण (birth-death cycle) से परे — पुनर्जन्म नहीं — मोक्ष।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'paramaṁ brahma-dhāma' = nirguṇa Brahman = the substratum of all. 'Viśvaṁ nihitam' = the universe rests IN Brahman — not Brahman in the universe. 'Akāmāḥ' = desireless knowers — free from desire. 'Śukram ativartanti' = they go beyond the birth-death cycle — no rebirth — mokṣa.
advaita.ins: The final teaching: the universe rests in Brahman, shining with Brahman's light. The wise — desireless, steady — transcend the very seed of rebirth. They don't go somewhere new. They realise where they've always been — in the supreme abode, where everything shines, where nothing is lacking, where the cycle ends.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'परमं ब्रह्मधाम' = भगवान् का दिव्य धाम — वैकुण्ठ — जहाँ विश्व शुभ्र (resplendent) है। 'अकामाः पुरुषं उपासते' = निष्काम भक्त — भगवान् की उपासना — भगवद्-प्रेम (divine love) ही साधन (means) और साध्य (end)। 'शुक्रम् अतिवर्तन्ति' = संसार-चक्र (cycle of rebirth) से मुक्ति — भगवान् के धाम को प्राप्ति।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'paramaṁ brahma-dhāma' = the Lord's divine abode — Vaikuṇṭha — where the universe shines resplendent. 'Akāmāḥ puruṣaṁ upāsate' = desireless devotees — worship of God — divine love is both the means and the end. 'Śukram ativartanti' = freedom from the cycle of rebirth — attainment of the Lord's abode.
vishisht.ins: The universe rests in God's supreme abode, shining with His radiance. The desireless devotees who worship Him — they transcend the cycle of birth entirely. Not through knowledge alone, not through action alone — but through love. Love without desire, worship without wanting — that is what takes you beyond.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'परमं ब्रह्मधाम' = सच्चिदानन्द (sat-cit-ānanda) — सत्य-चेतना-आनन्द — विश्व का आधार। 'भाति शुभ्रम्' = चेतना = प्रकाशमान (luminous) — जड़ नहीं। 'शुक्रम् अतिवर्तन्ति' = चेतना-विकास (evolution) का शिखर — अतिमानसिक रूपान्तर (supramental transformation) — जन्म-मृत्यु-चक्र से परे।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'paramaṁ brahma-dhāma' = sat-cit-ānanda — truth-consciousness-bliss — the ground of the universe. 'Bhāti śubhram' = consciousness = luminous — not inert. 'Śukram ativartanti' = the summit of consciousness-evolution — supramental transformation — beyond the cycle of birth and death.
aurobindo.ins: The universe shines in the supreme abode of consciousness — sat-cit-ānanda. It was never dark, never inert. The wise who worship the Person without desire — they transcend the very seed of becoming. They reach the summit of evolution — where consciousness knows itself fully, and the cycle of birth and death has no more hold.

dp.q: 🔍 The Muṇḍaka's conclusion — 'akāmāḥ' and 'dhīrāḥ'
dp.a: The Muṇḍaka Upanishad closes with two key words that summarise its entire teaching: 'Akāmāḥ' (desireless) and 'dhīrāḥ' (the wise/steady): 'Akāmāḥ' — the culmination of the desire-journey: the Muṇḍaka has traced the journey of desire through three stages: (1) Satya-kāma (3.2.3): lovers of truth — those whose desire is directed toward the real. This is the starting point — desire itself is not rejected but redirected. (2) Āpta-kāma (3.2.6): those whose desires are fulfilled — the sages who have found the Self and in it, all desire is satisfied. (3) A-kāma (3.2.11): desireless — those who have transcended desire entirely. Not by suppression but by fulfilment — when the Self is found, no desire remains because the source of all satisfaction is within. The progression is: desire for truth → fulfilment of desire → beyond desire. 'Dhīrāḥ' — the Upanishad's final word: the Muṇḍaka's last word is 'dhīrāḥ' — the wise, the steady, the resolute. This is the Upanishad's ideal: not the intellectual (paṇḍita), not the ritualist (yājñika), not even the ascetic (tapasvin) — but the 'dhīra': one who is firm in understanding, steady in vision, courageous in the pursuit of truth. The Kaṭha (1.2.1) uses the same word: 'parāñci khāni vyatṛṇat svayambhūḥ, tasmāt parāṅ paśyati nāntarātman, kaścid dhīraḥ pratyag-ātmānam aikṣat āvṛtta-cakṣuḥ amṛtatvam icchan' — 'Self-existent [Brahman] pierced the senses outward; therefore one sees outward, not the inner Self. Some rare dhīra, desiring immortality, turned the eyes inward and saw the Self.' The dhīra is the one who turns inward.

dp.q: 🔍 'Śukram ativartanti' — transcending the seed of rebirth
dp.a: The phrase 'śukram etat ativartanti' ('they transcend this luminous seed') is the Muṇḍaka's final statement about liberation: What is 'śukra'? (1) Literally: śukra = seed / semen / bright substance. It represents the generative principle — the creative force that produces bodies, births, and the continuity of saṁsāra. (2) Symbolically: śukra = the seed of becoming (bhava-bīja) — the karmic seed that germinates into future births. As long as this seed exists, the cycle of birth and death continues. (3) Philosophically: śukra = the creative impulse of Brahman that produces the world — 'tapasā cīyate brahma, tataḥ annam abhijāyate' (3.2.1). By transcending the śukra, the wise go beyond even Brahman's creative function. What does 'ativartanti' mean? 'Ativartanti' = they 'pass beyond' / 'transcend' / 'go beyond.' The wise don't merely escape the world — they transcend the very principle that generates worlds. They go beyond birth, beyond death, beyond becoming, beyond the cycle itself. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka parallel (4.4.6): 'When all the desires that lurk in the heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal — here he attains Brahman.' The 'śukra' (seed) is released, and with it, the last thread connecting the sage to the cycle of becoming is cut. The Muṇḍaka concludes: the wise — desireless, steady, knowers of the supreme abode — transcend the seed of rebirth and are free. This is the final word of the Muṇḍaka Upanishad.
